And when it came to choosing a place to study the language, traveling to Taiwan conveniently didn’t require her to apply for a visa. But on this quixotic mission to achieve total fluency, she finds that the gulf between her and her complicated family history won’t simply mend itself through diligent study. Her presumptions quickly unravel as she seeks answers in the gaps between economy seats on the flight from Boston to Taipei; in the uncertain, stilting words of Chinese heritage speakers; and in arthouse cinemas and concert halls she’s drawn to for the promise of blending in. From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of traveling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather—which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot—these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places. Condé Nast Traveler recently spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and being split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is available in bookstores now. This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity. Walk us through your research itinerary for Taipei Story. The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan. I was also in an intensive language program where I was wandering aimlessly around Taipei, meditating on [concepts of] home and cultural alienation. I wasn't walking around with a research agenda. I was just following crowds into places to see what they were seeing. If a long line of people was swarming, I would just join it. I would end up at screenings of movies I'd never heard of, or bookstores that I didn't know existed because I felt so blank, confused, and empty. I wanted somebody else to show me the answer to, “what is your city?” and if I became a ghost in its wake, was there a way I could totally erase myself? A lot of the descriptions in the novel where Lily ends up going to a place by accident, like the National Concert Hall, are places I also encountered by accident. Then, I started thinking about turning all those notes into an exaggerated, fictionalized version of what this experience would be—like if I were even younger and more dim-witted about how the world works. I read a lot of the major modern Taiwanese authors [like Kaori Li, Bai Xianyong, Chen Yingzhen, Wu Ming-yi, and Yang Shaung-zi—all mentioned in the author’s note and available in English translation] and wondered how they were thinking about home, identity, and being split between their mainland cultural heritage, and what it meant to be Taiwanese. How does this novel interface with—the sometimes impossible—expectations of homecoming? I'm fascinated with fantasies of homecoming and the narratives we buy into about how certain cultural experiences can return you to the fold. A lot of Chinese heritage speakers end up getting these flattened experiences in the US that feel like touch points, but are actually silly ways to reconnect—distilled cultural simulations such as Lunar New Year, red envelope parties, and film screenings. I say this not to mock diasporic kids; it makes total sense. You get so little, so you take whatever you can have, even if it's not region-specific or what your parents experienced. In Lily's case, I'm fascinated by the promises of heritage speaker-study abroad programs (editor’s note: these are linguistic immersion programs designed for students who grew up in households speaking a second language) because they hold so much promise and meaning for many people attending them. With Taiwan in particular, if you think about it just on the logical level, every step of this premise that you could, as a Chinese-American, go to Taiwan, to study Mandarin, to feel closer to your family on the mainland—is crazy. Lily's family has never been to Taiwan. She's the only person who's ever stepped foot there until her mom has a layover. When she finally gets there, she starts learning all the ways in which she is so wrong and how her experiences of Chineseness and the trajectory of her family history has absolutely nothing to do with Taiwan. In the end, she is a little more aware of this complexity and moves towards a more genuine, honest encounter of a strange place. She's like, I'm a foreigner, this is a weird summer, and maybe that's okay. In what ways does foreignness, or a lack of fluency, act as a source of fuel for travel and exploration in this novel? I definitely think [feeling out of place] is generative because I’ve felt like an outsider culturally for most of my life. My family immigrated [to the US from Guangzhou when Kuang was four-years-old], and I never felt like I quite belonged in the world of Dallas, Texas. I was a pretty happy kid, but when you're on the periphery, observing how people behave, I think you just get more perceptive. When I go back to China, that’s also not home, which is not a unique perspective. I think almost every immigrant kid feels this way. When I'm in China, I am looking at my family, and I observe cultural codes that they're following, and I have to figure out how these rules work because I didn't grow up understanding them innately. Being reflective about all of this makes you a good writer. In Lily's case I don't think she perceives her bumbling and ignorance as virtues. For her, it’s a barrier between her and the rest of the world. Because she's so afraid of getting things wrong, she never asks for help and never willing to embarrass herself. The ethical argument that the book is making is that embarrassment is really good for you. To admit, “I don't know what's going on,” and also “somebody helped me,” is an attitude I wish we all embraced more, not just when we're traveling, but in our entire lives. I find it a strength, and Lily finds it a weakness, and by the end of the book, she's at least accepted that she's gonna mess up, and she might as well own it. From the Poppy War trilogy to your last novel Katabasis, you often take on the perspective of being a student. Why return to the eyes of an undergraduate for this story? This book was very different because it's the first book of mine where the protagonists weren't growing up with me. When I was working on the Poppy War trilogy, I was a teenager, and they're teenagers, then they're undergrads, grad students, and in their late-20s. I was writing very reflexively to try to understand the world from my vantage point in life, but I had a couple of life changes in the past few years that made me more interested in going back. With the maturity of turning 30, I have more comfort in making fun of the person I used to be. When I was writing Taipei Story, it was like, I could write a memoir of what I experienced, or I could make things even more ridiculous, even more embarrassing, and reach back to the person I was when I was 18 going to Beijing for the first time and overwhelmed with everything I didn't know. The key to writing from the point-of-view of adolescence is not from this position of condescension that the youths are so silly, but to be kind to your younger self and recognize that all of your insecurities, all the things that you were failing at, everything that you got wrong, are deeply hilarious and also a really shared experience. There's a lot of humanity in cringe. By setting a story in modern-day Taipei, the narrative acknowledges Taiwanese-Chinese geopolitics, and beyond that, the country’s past with Japanese colonialism, the Chinese Civil War. How did you want to depict Taipei as a city with those layered histories? I wanted to be really cautious here, because I'm not Taiwanese. I'm not an expert in Taiwanese history or literature. As I pointed out in the author's note, this is not a voice from the inside but the very filtered perception of an American teenager who’s learning about all of this for the first time. I did want to poke gentle fun at the way that people generally take Western ideological frameworks that are very binary and project them onto local histories with no attention to what locals are actually saying. There's the first chapter where her little cohort of friends are running around the city, and there’s a pecking order based on assumptions about race. People would ask her where should we go? What should we eat? And she’d always pretend to know the answers and go Google them in the bathroom. They do the same thing when they're at Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall trying to understand, is he a good guy or a bad guy? Is he like George Washington? Should we be taking selfies with him? I wanted to give the experience of somebody who feels like they ought to be an expert by virtue of the ethnicity that they were born into, but who’s actually totally detached from genuine knowledge of the place or history. How did grief form your characterization of Taipei? [When Lily’s grandfather passed] it was a snapping moment for her. Up until that point, she is trying to slot all of her experiences into this predetermined narrative that this is getting her closer to the person she could have been if her family had never left China. After her grandfather passes, she is thrown into this weird grief and confusion, and she gives up on that goal altogether. She recognizes the futility of trying to go back and becoming a version of herself that never existed. Paradoxically, this frees her up to take in the things she closed her mind off to before. Now, she's okay with being a tourist. She goes on these Klook experiences [to Pinglin Tea Museum and Yehliu Geopark]. She’s on a bus with American families from Philly doing all the canned, predetermined activities just thinking, “oh, this is fun,” and learning a lot. Despite all the complex grief that is in this novel, it’s also very funny. Is Taipei a place that is particularly funny to you or has its own language of humor that you wanted to capture here? I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them. One in particular I'm obsessed with is Taiwan English. I was inspired by a blog post by Tao Lin, an author who also wrote a novel called Taipei. It was just a series of pictures that he took walking around of ridiculous translations, and some of them are accurate on a very literal, character-by-character level, and some of them, I can't believe you would get this result if you ran it through any translation app. But it's not just in Taiwan either. You see it on the mainland. For instance, my mom was wearing a shirt, that just said, “GO FUCK” in repeating block letters. She bought it at a clothes market with her sister when she was in China, and she was only paying attention to the fabric, and she was like, “Oh, it's so lovely. Does this color look good on me?” and didn't register the text at all. I said, “Mom, do you know what that says?” She turned it inside out and wore it that way for the rest of the day.

item.title: You Can Now Book the 'Sterling Point' Cottage on Airbnb—and the Inside Might Surprise You
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.02
Great news for anyone who fell in love with Muskoka after watching Sterling Point but didn't inherit a lake house from their estranged grandfather: Gordon Bay Cottage, the actual property at the center of the hit show, is officially coming to Airbnb. In the Prime Video series, protagonist Annie Rubin makes a pilgrimage to the property—located on a fictional island called Sterling Point—after finding out it has been willed to her after the death of her grandfather, Gordon. Now, fans will be able to call this same cottage home, at least for a few nights, thanks to an Airbnb sweepstakes allowing guests to request one of three special stays at the five-bedroom lakeside lodge this fall. Bookings open on September 15 at 9 a.m. ET, and the stays will take place October 2 to 5, October 9 to 12, and October 16 to 19, with a price tag of $180 a night. If you're looking to cosplay as Annie, Ellis, Connor, or Ramona, set your alarm now—these dates are going to go quick. While Gordon Bay Cottage serves as the façade for Gordon's cottage, interior scenes were filmed on a soundstage in Toronto, about two hours south of Muskoka. That means while the outside of the home will look familiar—cedar-shingled gables, wraparound porch, stone steps leading down to the water, Muskoka chair–dotted dock—the interiors aren't what you'd expect. In fact, they're way more upscale. While Gordon's place in the show looks like it hasn't been updated in a few decades, the property up for grabs on Airbnb appears fresh and modern, with hardwood floors, bright white walls, and contemporary but comfortable furniture. Probably not Ramona's style, but definitely ideal for a luxurious long weekend on the lake. The real Gordon Bay Cottage also sits right on Lake Joseph, one of the most popular and sought-after lakes in the Muskoka region, which means a stay here will come with all the trappings of a classic Canadian summer getaway. Sweepstakes winners should come with their Roots sweatpants and be prepared to “shower” in the lake, drink some Steam Whistles around the firepit, drive their boats to dinner, and gulp down some fresh air while staring at the stars. Ready to experience all that cottage country has to offer but afraid you won't be able to score a stay at Gordon Bay Cottage? Lucky for you, there are plenty of other incredible rentals in Muskoka, and we've found the best of the best. Between Sterling Point, Heated Rivalry, and Every Year After, this stunning slice of Ontario is more popular than ever (no, really, Airbnb searches from outside Canada for check-ins through November 2026 are up nearly 110% year over year, according to the vacation rental brand), so if you want to secure a lakeside spot for next summer, you'd be wise to start looking—and booking—now.

item.title: 7 Best Places in Costa Rica for Surfing, Sloth Sightings, and Tico Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.71
Costa Rica is one of those special places where the opportunities for exploration and adventure are nearly as diverse as the flora and fauna (which is arguably the most diverse on the planet). Whether you’re going for the yoga, to birdwatch, to surf, to explore the rainforest, dip in a hot spring, scuba dive, or climb a volcano, you’ll find it all there, along with delicious, healthy food, and accommodations to suit every taste. It’s rare for people to just visit just once. Instead, most people seem to fall in love with it and return over and over, either to old favorite spots, or to sample a new flavor of the experiences to be had. While a full book couldn’t do justice to all you can see there, here are a handful of highlights which you can use as a jumping off point for your exploration of this incredible land. Arenal & La Fortuna It’s hard to picture a better-balanced combination of adventure and relaxation. The town of La Fortuna makes an idyllic base for your exploration of Arenal volcano. Here you will find hot springs galore, white water rafting, rainforest canopy tours, paddling or windsurfing in Lake Arenal, and La Fortuna Waterfall (a 200-foot cascade you can swim right up to). La Fortuna has plenty of restaurants to keep your energy up, too. Where to stay nearby: The original hot springs resort with a natural river of thermal water running through it: Tabacón Thermal Resort & Spa. Eighteen thermal pools terraced into a hillside, plus an on-site wildlife rescue center: The Springs Resort & Spa. Nosara Where surf culture and wellness don’t so much as collide but coexist, Nosara is a laid-back beach town, full of yoga retreats, healthy and delicious restaurants, and plenty of waves. Playa Guiones is one of the most consistent beach breaks on the planet, and there are dozens of surf schools, camps, and a variety of waves for beginners to experts. Read our full guide to Nosara here. Where to stay nearby: For stunning views and one of the best restaurants in the country: Tierra Magnifica. For quick access to the beach and the heart of town: Sendero Nosara. For half hotel, half condo, featuring luxe rooms with an eye toward families: Silvestre Nosara. Manuel Antonio While much of the wildlife in Costa Rica requires going way off the beaten path, Manuel Antonio National Park is a major exception. It boasts some of the most dense populations of sloths, squirrel monkeys, toucans, white-faced capuchins, and many, many more. It’s laced with mellow coastal trails and absolutely jaw-dropping beaches, and the nearby town of Quepos has all the amenities one could want, plus nearby Tico cuisine at Rico Tico Jungle Grill's outdoor deck overlooking the treetops. Where to stay nearby: For luxury, views, and direct beach access: Arenas del Mar Beachfront & Rainforest Resort. For a romantic, adults-only, design-forward, boutique hotel: Makanda by the Sea San José Don’t treat the capital city as a mere layover. San José and the surrounding Central Valley will reward your curiosity, especially if you’re a coffee lover, as this is the region some of the world’s best beans come from. There are plenty of plantation tours around the still-active Poás and Irazú volcanoes, just a short daytrip away. The city itself is bursting with arts, culture, and one of the best and most innovative food scenes in Central America. You can walk off your meals exploring the Gold Museum, the resplendent 1897 National Theater, and plenty of public art and murals. Where to stay nearby: For a luxurious converted mansion in the heart of downtown book Hotel Grano De Oro. For quick access to the best restaurants and shopping in the city there’s InterContinental Costa Rica. For an only-in-Costa-Rica experience at a working coffee plantation with gorgeous architecture outside of the city; Finca Rosa Blanca Monteverde A stunning, green realm where the clouds seem to get caught in the canopy of the giant trees, Costa Rica’s premiere cloud forest is truly a thing to behold. It’s the birding capital of Costa Rica (which makes it one of the birding capitals of the world), and it’s here that you might catch a glimpse of the rare and majestic Resplendent Quetzal. The Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve, the Santa Elena Reserve, and the Curi-Cancha Reserve (all closely nestled) offer some of the richest wildlife-spotting hiking in the country, and there are some killer coffee tours, too. Where to stay nearby: For a Swiss-style chalet in the middle of the cloud forest, Hotel Belmar. For sustainable luxury with a private wildlife reserve, Hotel Belmar. Puerto Viejo & the South Caribbean Coast A whole different side of Costa Rica from the more-visited west coast, both literally and figuratively. Here you’ll find a mélange of Afro-Caribbean, Bribri indigenous, and Latinx influences, and that really shows up in the mouth-watering food and the local music scene. Puerto Viejo is the central town, full of bars, restaurants, shops, but it’s close to everything from the Gandoca-Manzanillo Wildlife Refuge (a hotspot for nesting turtles), a sloth reserve, a Jaguar Rescue Center, and the absolutely pumping waves of the notorious Salsa Brava surf break. Where to stay nearby: For individually curated Caribbean-Victorian beach bungalows: Hotel Aguas Claras. For a white-washed, design-focused property near the beach: Le Caméléon Boutique Hotel Corcovado & the Osa Peninsula Last but most definitely not least, a visit to Corcovado National Park is on the bucket list of any nature-lover. This rainforest was dubbed "the most biologically intense place on Earth" by National Geographic, and you will see why very quickly upon arrival as your chances are excellent for spotting tapirs, scarlet macaws, all four Costa Rican monkey species, and maybe even a jaguar. Getting there isn’t for the faint of heart, as it typically takes a puddle jumper or a very long drive followed by a boat to get way out there on the Osa Peninsula, and accommodations skew more glamping than luxurious, but if you make the pilgrimage, you will be rewarded by thin crowds and one of the most immersive nature experiences on planet Earth (and there’s good surf, too). Where to stay nearby: The peninsula's flagship eco-lodge on a private 1,000-acre reserve: Lapa Rios Ecolodge. The only luxury property with direct access to the gulf (boat trip required to get there) is Playa Cativo Lodge. Indonesian-style bungalows and beachfront access near Drake Bay: Copa de Árbol Beach & Rainforest Resort.

item.title: 7 Famous Homes From Movies and TV Shows You Can Actually Rent, Including Harry Potter’s Childhood Home and the 'Bachelor' Mansion
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.64
If you’ve ever dreamed of waking up in Bella Swan’s moody Forks home, where a vampire might pop in to say hello at any moment, or planning a Girls-style weekend trip out to Long Island’s North Fork, there’s a world of movie-famous rentals out there for turning your fictional fantasies into a reality. The seven properties on this list span famous homes from film and television, from Harry Potter’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow to the Bachelor mansion in Agoura Hills. Whether you’re looking to relive your favorite series or cosplay as a main character, these rentals have a certain star quality—after all, it took many professional location scouts to find them. From whimsical lofts in Tokyo fit for solo travelers to Cornwall, England, mansions that double as wedding venues, there’s a recognizable rental below for every kind of travel scenario. Just be sure to book ahead; these famous sets fill up fast. Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, shared bathroom Why we love it: Courtyard view, wood-burning fireplace, backyard Featured in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part One, the Vere House serves as Harry’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow. But its history can be traced back to the 15th century, when the De Vere family built it as a hunting lodge; the front door, with its medieval wooden carvings, is one of the most photographed sites in Lavenham, a village in Suffolk. The house features four en suite bedrooms (another is available to rent here), with access to the shared sitting room, where guests can gather and enjoy a roaring fire (and some crumpets, marshmallows, and sweet chestnuts in the winter months), or the courtyard when the weather’s nice. You’ll also have the option to order a full English breakfast, enjoyed in the communal dining room surrounded by centuries-old objects and artwork. Location: Lavenham, England Things to do nearby: The Crooked House, Six Bells Preston, Great Cornard Country Park Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 baths Why we love it: Proximity to riverfront, film memorabilia, patio While it’s booked out for months, Bella Swan’s home from Twilight is out there—not in Forks, but St. Helens, Oregon. And it never left 2008: The home is remarkably similar to the way it appears in the film, down to Bella’s purple floral bedspread (while not available for use, it is on display). Though the movie makes it seem like close quarters between Bella and Charlie, the house actually contains five bedrooms for you and your seven closest Twihards to spread out across. One reviewer wrote, “Watching the Twilight movies while staying in the house is every teenage girl's dream, and I can't believe it happened to me!” Location: St. Helens, Oregon Things to do nearby: St. Helens Historic Riverfront District, Historic Columbia Theatre, Crooked Creek Brewery Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, 1 bath Why we love it: Quirky architecture, indoor fireplace, in-unit washer/dryer Season five, episode three of Girls, simply titled “Japan,” is a world unto itself, and Shoshanna’s cartoon-like home away from home is no different. A jungle gym of sorts, the loft is decked out in primary colors, with bulbous fixtures and a wraparound layout. The bathroom, for instance, is housed in its own circular pod, while the kitchen sits in a central pit. This is a personal unit within a shared residential building, so guests might run into each other along common walkways and staircases. Quirky design lovers, this one’s for you. Location: Tokyo, Japan Things to do nearby: Nogawa Park, Ghibli Museum, Fuchu Art Museum Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 4 baths Why we love it: Beach access, pet-friendly, private pool Of the North Fork, Marnie from Girls says, “It’s for people who think the Hamptons are tacky and don’t want to be on a beach that’s near a J.Crew.” Once a Coast Guard lifesaving station built in 1893, the East Marion home that fueled one of the most iconic episodes in the show’s history is available to rent. But that’s not the property’s only claim to fame; the home also appeared in The Undoing, when Grace (played by Nicole Kidman) flees to the beach after her husband (Hugh Grant) goes missing. Right on the Long Island Sound with its own private slice of sand, this spacious home has enough room for up to 13 guests (hopefully your bachelorette weekend is more synchronized dance, less fighting). Location: East Marion, New York Things to do nearby: Orient State Park, Kontokosta Winery, town of Greenport Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Private pool, hot tub, mountain view Bachelor fans will revel in a stay at Villa de la Vina, the 10,000-square-foot Mediterranean-style mansion nestled within the Santa Monica Mountains of Malibu. You and 12 other guests can spread out across seven bedrooms and get a real-life glimpse of your favorite moments from the show. Whether you compete for love is up to you (may we suggest a bachelorette weekend instead?), but the romantic archways, infinity pool, and Agoura Hills views are sure to make you feel like you’re on a reality TV show. Bonus: Chef-prepared meals, airport transfers, and a chauffeur service are all available upon request. Location: Agoura Hills, California Things to do nearby: Liberty Lane Farms, Ladyface Trailhead, Malibu Wine Hikes Number of guests: 4–6 Bed and bath: 2–4 beds, 1–2 baths Why we love it: Film memorabilia, guided tours, gift shop While the house from A Christmas Story is available for daily tours in Cleveland, real fans of the beloved holiday classic will want to stay overnight in suites styled after the film, including the main house (lovingly restored) or the neighboring Bumpus House. All rooms are decked out in 1940s “hillbilly chic” interiors, and the loft, located in the main house, is where two lucky guests can sleep in Ralphie and Randy’s beds. Be sure to plan ahead, as these coveted rentals get booked up quickly around the holidays, and don’t leave without buying a pair of pink bunny pajamas in the gift shop. Location: Cleveland, Ohio Things to do nearby: Rowley Inn gastropub, Hooper Farm, Lincoln Park Number of guests: 21 Bed and bath: 12 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Seaview rooms, proximity to beach, grand piano, game room Ideal for an English seaside wedding, the Porthpean House is as romantic as it gets, not least because it was featured in the cult-favorite 2013 film About Time. Overlooking Porthpean Beach, the salt-sprayed home was originally built in 1793 and has belonged to the Petherick family for five generations before becoming a dreamy vacation rental. Sleeping up to 21 guests, it houses several historic rooms, including a drawing room, gaming room, dining room, multiple kitchens, and an office, as well as acres of fresh lawn to frolic around. Location: Cornwall, England Things to do nearby: Porthpean Beach, Porthpean Golf Club, RAF Quadrant Tower

item.title: What Rockaway Film Festival Can Teach Us About Going to the Movies
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.63
Despite its endless appetite for novelty, New York City really is a creature of recursion. Memories never remain too far behind, or rather, too far ahead, before they’re back again wearing a familiar form. One of the city’s finest resurrections in recent memory is moviegoing in the Rockaways. Like the millionaire colonies born of Gilded Age excesses or the Coney Island-rival Rockaways’ Playland that formerly occupied this area of coastal Queens, it’s a stretch of the imagination to conjure up the heyday of movie theaters by the beach. Their near-absence on the peninsula today obscures the foreign era they once thrived in, a few golden decades that spanned from the 1920s to ‘50s earmarked by 25-cent tickets to double features, smoking-friendly cinemas, and faux tuxedoed attendants. A combination of factors ranging from demographic shifts following the Second World War to devastating building fires to general neighborhood decline led to the gradual shuttering of Rockaways’ theaters. The last gasp came when Jerry Lewis Cinema closed its doors in 1996, and the Rockaways went without a commercial indoor theater for the next 25 years. The dry spell was finally broken in 2021 by the nonprofit Rockaway Film Festival organization, when it led the effort of building Arverne Cinema, now the only one of its kind. Ever since the festival itself started nine years ago—popping up screens in venues from Fort Tilden to Jacob Riis Park—hope for the return of moviegoing as a neighborhood pastime has abounded, as one might expect following any reported sighting post-extinction. I arrive at this year’s Rockaway Film Festival (RFF9) in local uniform, with swim trunks donned beneath my work slacks and flip-flops afoot in case of any impromptu beach-going. With the day’s storms recently broken, the muggy summer air made way for a preview of the better days of fall to set the stage for an evening at the open-air movies. The outdoor cinema is wrapped by a rough-hewn Brutalist perimeter—half-lined with concrete cubes, the other half enclosed with planks salvaged from the boardwalk destroyed during Hurricane Sandy. Filled with gravel and sand, it’s like we’re on the bottom of a riverbed with the constant stream of smooth-bellied airplanes taking off above us from the nearby JFK airport. The space certainly feels scrappier than the black-and-white photos of its predecessors. For one, the former Arverne Theater—once a venue for Yiddish acts from the Rockaways’ vibrant Jewish community—broadcasted itself with an outsized vertical marquee until its dismantling in 1952. And the Arverne Pier Theater wore its neoclassical inspirations on its sleeve, complete with Corinthian columns and a half-round pediment. The main centerpiece of the cinema that stands today is its screen, and behind it, there’s not much in the way of scenery. Peeping over the horizon, tower cranes hover forever paused in their progress at the defunct concrete facility, leaning over with their trussed necks, a family of mechanical sauropods. The warmth of the space only truly activates once it’s brimming with people: within my earshot, some trade stories on their convoluted commutes to get here; others debate the ethics of documentary-making; but most exchange reports on what they’ve seen recently and the homework they’ve done on what’s about to screen. Though, those conversations might only apply to the crowd for the world premiere of Eternity One, a documentary from Baltimore-based filmmaker Marnie Ellen Hertzler regarding the precarity of Tangier Island, a remote island community in the Chesapeake Bay eroding from the climate crisis. While the film is the first screening of the festival, it’s not necessarily indicative of the programming (or the crowds) to come. The exciting truth is that none of the films quite are, with the RFF9 lineup reading as an eclectic yet affordable menu. Tickets are capped at $10, and a handful of movies are even being shown for free to ensure that everyone who wants a seat can get one. To name but a few of the movies showing, there’s the 1979 Muppets Movie (the one with “Rainbow Connection”), a generational crowd-pleaser sure to work its magic once again with young families in attendance; a collection of animated shorts themed around “Romantasy” for the old school Adult Swim crowd; and a Dabke dance workshop led by El Funoun, a traditional Palestinian dance company braiding celebration with resistance. As the latter item suggests, there’s much more to the festival than just what’s on screen. Most movies are paired with local live acts to fill the air as the crowd mills in or to keep the party going long after the projector shuts off. You might walk into one screening to the processional music of Brooklyn slacker prog and exit the next to a Roots reggae DJ set. Kyp Malone, in all his braid-bearded glory, plays before Eternity One, at times playfully directing us, “now pretend I’m a movie, and pay the fuck attention,” and later offering light conversation starters between straight-from-the-bottle sips of Casamigos like, “did you think fascism was going to feel different?” One particularly inspired pairing comes from the combination of Ridgewood-based documentarian John Wilson’s first feature, The History of Concrete, with a set from Bellerose rapper Heems (of Das Racist fame for any lovers of combination Pizza Hut-Taco Bells). Wilson’s whispering, Kermit-ish cadence juxtaposed with Heems’s audacious bars shorthands the borough’s rejection of one-size-fits-all characterization as one of the most diverse urban centers in the world. Tying a bow on the Queens-ness of it all is the al-fresco setting itself. This might be the one pocket of the city that does sleep. Call it the influence of the local surf culture, or the protected peace of the nearby nature reserves, but the Rockaways are just the kind of place made for prying sticks out of asses. Take it from friendly neighborhood rockstar Patti Smith, who put it simply on her Substack: “Being at Rockaway Beach makes me happy.” It’s long ceased to be a neighborhood that puts on airs, an attitude that liberates us all tonight. Under the darkening sky, I’m oddly comforted by the couple next to me taking advantage of the shifting tenebrism for some drive-in-style PDA. Tucked inside the cul-de-sac of a residential street off of Beach 67, Arverne Cinema is right at home amongst the two-story houses hosting their own celebrations, with one particularly passionate birthday party across the street beating out the volume of Hertzler’s Q&A. While the festival bounced around for its first few years, finding a permanent home in the community had always been the goal. “There’s not much that’s like the joy of sharing a movie that you love very much in a space that was built by friends and neighbors with a full audience,” said RFF co-founder and organizer Courtney Muller, reflecting on the festival’s sixth year at Arverne Cinema. At the risk of sounding like another trite moral about the importance of social gathering post-pandemic, the Rockaway Film Festival is as much about movie-going as it is about movie-watching. Thankfully, the act is not nearly as endangered as it was once reported to be, with chains like AMC boasting booming attendance numbers. But factors such as surging ticket prices and shorter gaps between theatrical runs and streaming releases contribute to the perception that going out to the movies is a luxury, and shrink crowds accordingly. That image is only bolstered by the glamorous superlatives we’ve come to expect from premiere film festivals around the world—the record-smashing standing ovations at Cannes, a bigger and better revamp of Sundance, the making or breaking of Oscar contenders at the Toronto International Film Festival. Between the flimsy baskets of superb beach shack grub and seating reminiscent of a school play, the Rockaway Film Festival is doing the remedial work of bringing movies back to the people by reminding its attendees that a movie theater is not supposed to be a sarcophagus. My favorites in New York, and the ones I’d champion are worth traveling for, are all framed by their own signs of life, from the faint roar of the subways that rumbles through the Angelika to the shoulder-to-shoulder sardine can theaters of Film Forum (though one should never go so far as to condone cellphone use for QR code ordering at an Alamo Drafthouse). That a film festival grows in the Rockaways after more than two decades without a single theater is a feat in its own right, and its longevity for the past nine years speaks to the simple human desire shared by cinephiles and curious locals alike that watching a good movie in a crowd of peers, perhaps even with your toes in the sand, should come at no exorbitant cost. “When this festival began as a four-day experiment in 2018, it was not just about showing movies—it was about saying clearly to this community that it deserves cinema,” shared Rafael Espinal, Commissioner of the Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment, to kick off the start of this year’s events, “Rockaway reminds us that cinema belongs everywhere in New York City, not just in the places where people expect them, but right here, by the beach with this community.” In an interview with Hell Gate, Muller described the undercurrent of this year’s programming as the “stories of things coming apart” and what grows in the spaces left after collapse. It might as well be the unofficial motto for the Rockaways, where surfers dropped everything to shovel out sunken homes after Hurricane Sandy, grassroots mutual aid networks opened their doors to displaced New Yorkers after 9/11, and neighbors came together to convert a vacant lot into a movie theater. RFF9 is an exemplary case study that the local flavor of the Rockaways is best appreciated up close. I can’t write about what it was like to taste the salt air seasoned with New York atmosphere and make the flavor materialize on your tongue. A high-budget documentary exclusive to the streaming platform that produced it can’t either. You might have to wait another year for the next festival, take the A train as far down as you’ve ever taken it, come early, and claim one of the beach chairs while you can to feel it for yourself, but the point is that you must. How to Visit Rockaway Film Festival This year's festival runs from September 2-6, and while tickets to the remaining screenings have all sold out online, some have limited capacity for tickets sold at the door, and for others, you can sign up to be on a waitlist at the ticket stand before showtime. For the most up-to-date information on this year's screenings, visit the programming page of the festival here. As far as getting yourself to Arverne Cinema, you have a few options. You could take the Far Rockaway-bound A train to Beach 67 and walk eight minutes to the theater, ride the Q22 bus to the Rockaway Beach Blvd / Beach 73 St stop or the Beach Channel Dr / Beach 71 St stop (and connect to the bus from the LIRR Far Rockaway station), or ride the NYC Ferry, which by and large offers the most scenic views. The festival's website also hosts an extensive Rockaway guide with recommendations ranging from where to get your morning coffee to the best cannabis dispensary in town. Take full advantage of these expert recs by basing yourself directly in the Rockaways. For a weekend stay, the beachy sanctuary of the Rockaway Hotel is the way to go.

item.title: 26-Time US Open Tennis Star Venus Williams on Paris, Partying, and the Perfect Pair of Heels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.50
If there’s one thing about Venus Williams, it’s that she has stamina. The seven-time Grand Slam singles champion is currently playing in her 26th US Open—making more appearances than any other player in tennis history. The California-born athlete played her first professional match at just 14, meaning she’s been not just a tennis pro, but also a travel pro, for more than three decades. With life constantly on the road, she admits that her idea of vacation is when she gets to relax at her Florida home. But that also means that she prioritizes comfort when it comes to hotels, opting for ones with a homey feel. “I do not compromise on hotels,” the 46-year-old told Condé Nast Traveler during a pre-US Open event at The Langham, New York, Fifth Avenue. “I will compromise on my flight and sit almost anywhere, it doesn’t matter to me. But I just have to be at an amazing hotel.” She admits that when she was younger, she was lured by the “newest, coolest, trendiest” design-forward accommodations. But now, she opts for “extremely established hotels that have amazing service”—plus a "beautiful bed.” While she mused about her favorite city in the world being Hong Kong (she’s contemplating a fall tournament there just to revisit) and her enthusiastic passion for escape rooms (her favorites include The Escape Game, Escapology, and PanIQ, but her goal is to compete in the World Escape Room Championships. which was last in Bulgaria), Williams chose to hone in on a trip to Paris, a city that has helped her redefined her life’s priorities. The trip What trip are you unpacking for us? There have been many trips to Paris Fashion Week, but let’s go back to the one in the winter of 2024, before I was married. I was going to go to one or two shows. Two, for me, is a lot. It involves a ton of getting ready. And on this trip, I took my sister Isha. Can you tell us more about the itinerary? I try to fit in gym sessions here and there, some tennis as well. But most of all, I know I’ll be out every night, so I have to bring clothes to be ready for my nightlife, which is extremely important. Had you been to Paris before? My first time in Paris, I was 16 years old playing the French Open. So in that sense, I go at least once a year. But during this time, I really wasn't working, so I was constantly in Paris. I had this streak where I was there every month for like six months in a row. It finally broke. I was so sad. I just love Paris—it’s such a magical city for me. What makes the city so special? A few years before this, the French Open, which always happens in May, was in October during the pandemic. They put us in a bubble. We were only allowed to have a one-hour walk a day. So once I unfortunately did lose at the tournament. I checked myself into a luxury hotel and started shopping and partying. This was before the second shutdown. Paris became my new favorite city, as it represented freedom and choice. I hadn’t done much in my life out of the court. A friend of mine said, “You should come to the Louis Vuitton show” and I was like, “I gotta get home.” But I went to the show, and it felt like my whole life got started. What she packed What do you usually wear on a flight? It depends on how I feel. If I want to be chic, a cardigan and a turtleneck. I used to always fly in Ugg boots—they’re not that popular now, so I'm like the only one wearing them. Other than that, I love Wolford leggings and definitely a long-sleeved sweater since I'm always cold. Most unusual thing you pack for every trip? A karaoke mic! It’s got to be a quality mic. My family is a karaoke family and you never know when you need the mic. I don't have a go-to song—I have a whole list! The last one was probably “Danger Zone” by Kenny Loggins. My husband loves Michael Jackson, but I’ve learned a few Italian songs from him—we do an Italian duet. [My sister] Serena likes to do The Little Mermaid’s “Part of Your World.” She likes Disney standards. What clothes did you pack? I'll bring two to three workout outfits from Lacoste. I figure I can wash them. I'm probably not gonna be doing cardio. It's most likely going to be strength training, so I could maybe wear it over again. I was more concerned about my evening outfits. I was a single girl. I'm wearing short dresses and preparing for any and every party that I don't even know I'm gonna be at. So then, we have to ask: what shoes did you bring? My heels—the ones that I can dance in and still wear for hours because I love dancing. Christian Louboutin 80 centimeters were my go-tos. They’re high. I’m 6-foot-1 and I love being tall. I’m not afraid of it. What other scenarios did you pack for? I brought one Wilson racquet—that's not a lot of racquets. On another trip, when I was kind of down and out on my own tennis career, I didn't even bring a racquet. Then I suddenly realized I wanted to play tennis and had to get one, which was challenging. I managed to get one of Serena's racquets! Otherwise, I didn't really repeat outfits, so I always had to have something a little bit new. I was also going on dates—many of them not serious at all. But I had to have my date outfits for the daytime, possibly even a lunch date. Which outfit did you wear first? The night we got in, my sister and I were done because we already had to get up in like four hours. We’d taken showers, washed our hair, and put on face masks— all the things. Then a friend texts that there’s a party in so-and-so’s room. I ask my sister if we should go, and she’s awful and says yes. So I grab a Louis Vuitton shift dress. I don't know how I got my hair together so fast, and here's the thing: I didn't take the mask off. It was a clear Tata Harper resurfacing mask—the pink jelly one! So how was the party? The hotel was close, so we ran in the freezing winter night and there was nothing happening at this party! There was one guy there who had a crush on me, but he was not someone you would ever date. Finally we went home and had to wake up two hours later feeling miserable and start hair and makeup for the show. This was my lifestyle and I loved it—I got to live it! I’m not living it now, but that was when you’ve got to have that second outfit ready for that very random moment! What souvenirs did you buy on this trip? Well, I used to have a major shopping addiction. So I took home pretty much everything in Paris. My motto at the time was, "I'm not winning, but I'm spending." I was laughing until the credit card bill came, and then it wasn't funny anymore. I bought watches that I've never worn—that was bad. For the most part, I try to buy timeless things. I don't shop anymore, but deep down I'm just waiting for that moment where I start up again. It's not today. It's not tomorrow. I'm under control…for the moment. Have you found any jet lag cures? If you land at night, stay up on the flight. That rhymes. If you land during the day, go out and play. I'm a rapper now! But if I land in the day, I allow myself an hour or two nap, then I go to practice and stay up. The minimum is 10 o’clock. When you do that, you’ll pretty much be on the time zone. But if you allow yourself to just sleep, you're going to just be miserable. Is there something you bring with you as a piece of home when you're on the road? My dog Harold. He’s a 19-year-old Havanese. On this trip, did you over pack, under pack, or get it just right? Slightly overpacked. When I travel on short trips, I insist on just carry-on. It's very liberating. Packing for tennis is a little challenging because I have to pack my match clothes, practice clothes, and clothes for off the court. There are so many tennis shoes—you need at least two, in case one goes out. It’s happened to me and if you don’t have that second pair on the side, you’re screwed. You also need racquet string, an ice machine, and a bunch of stuff. So I travel with four bags—I give one to my husband, so it’s three, but it’s hard. Finally, what makes the US Open special compared to other Grand Slams? It’s a city that never sleeps. The energy here is so much that people who live here need to get out of the city—that says a lot! And the crowd is just boisterous, but once they're locked in, they're there for you. Then they're not leaving you. It’s just a very special experience.

item.title: 10 Best Coffee Shops in Seattle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.72
Seattle could probably coast on its coffee reputation for another half-century, but visitors who equate the Emerald City with the green mermaid miss out on its world-class selection of bright and bold brews. Those live in the independent shops and local roasters that keep Seattle awake for the longest of summer days, and perky through the dark, damp winters. Whether you’re on a pilgrimage to this birthplace of American latte art (at Espresso Vivace), looking to be transported to the cutting edge of specialty coffee (at Slow Day Coffee), or you just want drip and a breakfast sandwich while you get your bike fixed (at Peloton Bicycle Shop & Cafe), this city has the perfect cup for you—here's where to find the best coffee shops in Seattle. Read our full Seattle travel guide here, which includes: - The Best Things to Do in Seattle - The Best Hotels in Seattle - The Best Restaurants in Seattle - The Best Bars in Seattle How we choose the best coffee shops in Seattle Every bar on this list has been selected independently by Condé Nast Traveler editors and reviewed by a local contributor who has visited that coffee shop. Our editors consider both high-end and affordable cafés, and weigh stand-out dishes, location, and service—as well as inclusivity and sustainability credentials. We update this list as new bars open and existing ones evolve. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Boston’s Best Lobster Rolls Include a Secret Off-Menu Pick
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.62
New Englanders grow up on unfussy seafood like lobster rolls the way other people grow up on tacos or barbecue—foods so embedded in the way of life of a particular place that you don’t realize how special they are until you start traveling. Now, when I’m away from home, I find that lobster rolls are seen as an expensive delicacy. Yes, lobster rolls are special; they exist in the city’s glitzier and fine-dining restaurants, and their prices have skyrocketed in more recent years. But they’re also just as common at fast food counters in the suburbs and fishmonger docks up and down the coast. And just like paying $6 a gallon for gas on a California road trip, or $43 for a martini at Bemelman’s Bar in Manhattan, having a lobster roll in Boston is a worthwhile investment every once in a while. It's simply what you do when you’re here. That being said, not all lobster rolls are created equal—and many (sometimes controversial) variations exist. A purist will say that a proper one must—must!—be served on a split-top bun that’s been griddled until golden brown, while others make compelling arguments for fancy swaps like brioche rolls. Then there’s the lobster meat itself, served either as a simply dressed cold salad (Maine style) or warm and buttered (Connecticut style)—but that’s more of a personal preference. The good news? There are many, many lobster rolls to experience in Boston, ranging from textbook classics to more chef-driven interpretations. Here's where to find the best. Row 34 Chef Jeremy Sewall knows a thing or two about good fish, and his popular Row 34 restaurants (with locations in Fort Point and in Cambridge’s Kendall Square) are where you go for excellent beer, interesting wines, and a chef’s sensibility. Here, the lobster roll is surprisingly personal, with lobster sourced from chef Sewall’s cousin Mark, who captains a boat in York Harbor, Maine. There are two versions here: a warm buttered roll with steamed tail, claw and knuckle meat and tucked into a traditional split-top bun; and the other, the Ethel’s Creamy Lobster Roll, named for Sewall’s grandmother and folded together with celery, red onion, pickles, mayonnaise, crème fraîche, lemon, celery salt and black pepper. The cold, creamy one comes on a rosemary brioche bun that is griddled to order and is nothing short of heavenly. James Hook & Co. James Hook & Co. is the alpha and omega of Boston lobster rolls; a platonic ideal of what a lobster roll should be. The family-run seafood business operating on the Boston waterfront for over 100 years is an adorable, unassuming shack on shiny, transformed Atlantic Avenue downtown—this is where any good lobster roll tour of the city should begin (or end). The company ships over 50,000 pounds of lobster daily, both online and to wholesale distributors nationwide, so they know a thing or two about quality. The rolls here come in two sizes and two styles, either chilled or warm with butter. While you’re here, don’t overlook the other seafood specialties; the double-stuffed scallop, clam chowder, and lobster mac and cheese make for a perfect shared side. Saltie Girl If James Hook is the lobster roll in its natural habitat, Saltie Girl is its glamorous, city-slicker cousin. This stylish Back Bay restaurant slings some of the best seafood on Newbury Street, in an elegant yet playful dining room overlooking the boutiques of Newbury Street. Its classic New England-style lobster rolls arrive perfectly coiffed, alongside a charmingly branded bag of Saltie Girl potato chips (add some caviar from the raw bar if you like). But the real insider move here? Ask your server about the secret, off-menu version of the lobster roll: the meat comes fried, sprinkled with Korean chili flakes and sweet corn butter, resulting in something richer, spicier, and considerably more decadent than a traditional version. It’s a sterling reminder that, even in a historic city like Boston, we don’t have to take our classics so seriously. The Banks Seafood and Steak The Banks is a crowd-pleaser of a restaurant—a perfect location in Back Bay, a lively bar scene, and an elevated menu of New England classics. The lobster roll here is an example of a perfectly adventurous recipe where the chef has improved on the original with a few tweaks, but none so heretical that they feel like a major departure from tradition. It comes on a house-made brown-butter bun, sprinkled with sea salt and chives, and served with Old Bay potato chips. The hot lobster roll is a standout—it’s par-cooked, then warmed in a “lobster beurre monté,” a classic French technique that glazes the meat and also helps infuse more lobster flavor into it. The result is a roll that is deceptively simple, yes, bursting with flavor. Eventide Fenway Originally from Portland, Maine, Eventide brought its contemporary take on New England seafood to the Fenway neighborhood as a seafood counter in 2017 before evolving into a full-service restaurant in 2023. The experience here is decidedly more Boston than Maine—it’s a bustling, popular spot for pre-Fenway Park drinks and snacks, less of a cozy, James Beard-recognized eatery than its progenitor in Portland—but Eventide did one key invention with it for the Hub: its brown butter lobster rolls. They come on a fluffy, bao-style steamed bun, drenched (in a good way) with browned butter and flecked with sliced chives. The Sail Loft Nestled on the fringes of the North End within steps of the Freedom Trail, Faneuil Hall and the restaurants of Hanover Street, this institution feels like it’s been here forever. The Boston Sail Loft’s lobster roll is classic, with chilled lobster salad lightly dressed with mayonnaise and piled generously into a toasted bun. The thick, crispy fries that accompany it are a departure from the canonical bag of chips, but they’re a nice touch. There are fancier lobster rolls in Boston—but with perfect execution, stiff drinks and waterfront views, what else would you need? Red’s Best at Boston Public Market A great, no-frills option for travelers who want to understand where their seafood actually comes from, this counter inside Boston Public Market is dedicated to small, independent New England fishermen. And that direct connection to the local fishing community is what makes this experience special. The market itself—just steps from the Freedom Trail—is an easy stop while sightseeing, especially if you’re in the Faneuil Hall, North End, or Beacon Hill areas. The lobster rolls fresh and unfussy. While there’s no waterfront view or white tablecloth, there is something very Boston about enjoying solid seafood in a bustling public market surrounded by Bostonians going about their everyday lives. Plus: Save room for a doughnut from Union Square Donuts, or a popover from The Popover Lady. The Barking Crab Right across Fort Point Channel from James Hook & Co., you’ll find The Barking Crab, another old-school spot where the lobster rolls are classic, but the atmosphere is decidedly more festive. This ramshackle seafood restaurant feels like a relic from the old Seaport, before the neighborhood redeveloped into an epicenter of glass towers and luxury condos. The location makes it especially appealing on warmer days, and the vibe is a little rowdy (in a good way). The lobster roll here is a straightforward expression—toasted roll, available either tossed with mayo or “naked” with warm, butter-poached lobster meat—but if you’re really feeling like splurging, opt for the “One and Done”: whereas most rolls come with about one-fourth a pound of meat, this one comes with a solid one pound, for a whopping $150. Worth it? After a few beers or cocktails, you bet. Yankee Lobster Co. Venture into the Seaport, keep cruising past all the newfangled developments, and you’ll eventually find yourself at Yankee Lobster Co., which has been serving seafood here for roughly 75 years, making it one of the increasingly rare links to the city’s working waterfront in this part of town. That history is part of the appeal, and the lobster roll is comfortingly old-school: generously portioned, straightforward, crafted from the freshest lobster. Come here if you want a classic Boston seafood experience without the polish or price tags of the Seaport’s flashier restaurants. Sullivan’s Castle Island A visit to Castle Island—which is actually not an island, but the tip of the peninsula known as South Boston, or “Southie”—is a beloved Boston ritual. You walk or bike to the far edge of Southie, go for a waterfront stroll around Fort Independence, the oldest continuously fortified site in British North America, then stop for a refueling at Sullivan’s, so much a part of the fabric of Boston life that it received a James Beard Foundation America’s Classics Award. This is not the lobster roll to choose if you’re looking for culinary drama—it’s the one you choose when you want to eat seafood like a Boston local.

item.title: The Best Hotels in Berlin at Every Price Point
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.58
More than three decades after the wall came down, Berlin remains a city in constant flux, where the past and present intertwine in wildly innovative ways. A booming capital brimming with youthful energy and creative ideas, it is reinventing itself brick by brick—and nowhere is this more evident than in its dynamic hotel scene. New life has been breathed into landmark properties, and dilapidated buildings have been rescued and refashioned into chic boutique stays. Famed global brands such as Rocco Forte and The Hoxton have arrived on the scene, joining timeless classics that have stood for the past century. From the splashy west to the grittier east, property choices in every style and at every price point span the city. Here are the best hotels in Berlin that are open for check-in now, as chosen by our local editors. Our top picks: - Best for luxury: Waldorf Astoria Berlin - Best for a central location: Telegraphenamt - Best for families: Michelberger Hotel - Read Full ReviewHoused in a late 19th-century building, Irish lifestyle hotel brand The Dean brings its “vibe first” philosophy to the German capital, pairing bold design with cultural connectivity and a food concept that draws in more than just overnight guests. Interiors channel Berlin’s creative energy and avant-garde spirit from the moment you step inside. Historic architectural details sit alongside saturated colors, sculptural lighting, and a confident, contemporary design language. Room numbers are handwritten on the doors rather than printed—an intentionally imperfect detail that nods to Berlin’s slightly rough-around-the-edges character. In the bathrooms, original black-and-white tiles have been preserved, punctuated by red shower frames and boldly framed mirrors. Toiletries are by D.S. & Durga, lending a subtle spa feel. For food, Benedict is the heart of the hotel—a bakery, restaurant, and bar combined in one lively, open space. Breakfast is served until 4 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends. The focus is, naturally, on eggs Benedict in multiple variations: with ham and cheese, avocado, or pulled beef, served on brioche or a buttery croissant. The brand’s Irish roots are also present in the drinks offering: whiskey in every minibar, the Irish cocktail “Ól,” and even a dedicated Guinness tap behind the bar—a small but unmistakable nod to its heritage. —Susanna Gunst - Read Full ReviewThis sophisticated hotel in Mitte’s bustling center, steps from the Brandenburg Gate, features one-of-a-kind guest rooms decorated by local and international artists. The prominent neon sign on the façade is strategically placed above a self-portrait done in bronze by artist Alicja Kwade, and once inside, you’re transported into a moodily lit living room reminiscent of an art patron’s salon. Refined couples, having just finished their cocktails, chat quietly while on their way out to the Staatsoper (German State Opera). It all feels very calm and grown up, like an idealized version of Berlin’s past artistic glories, updated with a buzzy sense of creative present. Bed down in a room with hand-painted wallpaper or a hand-carved folding screen; each is uniquely decorated and may have a one-of-a-kind large-scale painting on the wall, or even a funky video installation. Bathrooms are lined in glazed subway-style tiles and have heated floors and large walk-in showers. The property is an easy to walk to the Reichstag; if you’ve come to shop, Friedrichstrasse is a block away; to run or bike, the large green expanse of Tiergarten is a hop and a skip. —Liz Humphreys - Read Full ReviewWith an exceptional location on Monbijoupark in the Mitte district, this grand neo-Baroque building once housed the city’s vast telegraph office—built between 1910 and 1916, and at one time the most sophisticated postal building in Germany. It has since been meticulously restored and transformed into a posh destination for discerning travelers looking to stay close to a huge selection of trendy restaurants, bars, and shops, as well as beloved Hackesche Höfe's old courtyards-turned-commercial spaces. The 97 guest rooms all have an industrial look, with brick-barrel vaulted ceilings divided by metal beams and exposed brick walls. Art Deco design elements like illuminated glass capsules, which display the room numbers, nod toward the building’s history, and hanging lamps adorn each side of the bed like a movie star’s chandelier earrings. Though occupied by digital nomads during the day, the bar at ROOT buzzes after dark, and a DJ spins techno beats nightly starting at 8 p.m.—this is Berlin, after all. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewFans of the flagship Waldorf Astoria New York will feel right at home in this Berlin outpost, set in an elegant skyscraper in City West and just around the corner from the exclusive shopping boulevard Kurfürstendamm (Ku’damm). Rooms are seriously big—starting at 452 square feet—and designed in a contemporary style, with neutral gray velour furnishings, swirl-patterned rugs, and a statement-making gold wall behind the beds. Large marble bathrooms have separate tubs and showers in every category, and the in-mirror televisions and Aesop toiletries add a luxurious touch. Reached by a separate elevator, the Tower Suites (floors 22 to 31) are worth it for the views—of the city, the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, or the neighboring Tiergarten park and Berlin Zoo. For a true splurge, the massive 30th-floor Astor Suite (with floor-to-ceiling windows, a balcony, and a separate dining room and kitchen) or the 31st-floor Presidential Suite (complete with a grand piano, open fireplace, and two balconies) boast sweeping city views. —Jennifer Ceaser - Read Full ReviewA neoclassical 19th-century bank houses this five-star Rocco Forte property, which enjoys an unrivaled location on Bebelplatz, right in the historic heart of East Berlin. Many of the building’s original details—graceful marble columns, skylights, an intricate iron staircase—have been retained, most notably down below in the pool area, formerly the bank’s jewel vault. A contemporary design streak runs throughout the lobby, which is dotted with oversized black velvet sofas, towering red-lacquer vases, and dangling globe lights, plus a playful pink neon birdcage as the centerpiece. Book one of the higher-end suites and get perks galore, including personalized concierge service, luggage unpacking, free pressing of one garment, and in-house movies. There's a standard minibar in all rooms, but you can request a bespoke Rocco Forte Nourish minibar in advance, stocked with a selection of healthy snacks and drinks. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1891 as a private residence and converted into a hotel in 1911, Hotel Zoo has been one of West Berlin’s poshest stays for more than a century. In the 1950s, it served as the VIP hotel for the Berlin International Film Festival and was a haunt for A-listers like Grace Kelly and Sophia Loren. So it’s fitting that the hotel’s glamorous history has been reinterpreted by two Hollywood designers, Dayna Lee and Ted Berner. The cool design aesthetic and location on Ku'damm, Berlin's best shopping street, make it a covetable stay for anyone. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewToday, there’s that sense that Hotel Adlon Kempinski Berlin—having withstood the vicissitudes of a tumultuous century—is armor-plated, as unassailable as the bulletproof floor-to-ceiling windows of the presidential suites. Under the Kempinski aegis since the 1990s, it bottles that sense of timelessness and offers a feeling of security and tradition as something that is as precious as it is soothing. The past is present here, exuding patrician-style grandeur and elegance: the Art Deco floor gauges in the elevators, an old-fashioned bicycle that the bellboys use, the panels of walnut wood in the Michelin-starred Lorenz Adlon Esszimmer restaurant, acres of marble for a grand staircase, and gold flakes even on the lobby lounge’s currywurst. Old-school perfectionism calls for the three types of caviar and Champagne at breakfast, as well as butler-ironed newspapers brought to the table. It all contributes to that illusion that you are in a cocoon, away from the travails of the world. —Catherine Fairweather - Read Full ReviewKPM is the vision of Berlin banker Jörg Woltmann, who helped save the 18th-century Royal Porcelain Manufactory Berlin complex on which the hotel has stood since 2019. The ultra-modern, cube-like building has picked up multiple design and architecture prizes and was nominated as Europe’s Leading Design Hotel by the 2021 World Travel Awards. Rooms are minimalist, chic, and smartly designed, with functional desks, high-tech wall control panels, and clever built-ins that make the spaces seem larger than they are—aided by the floor-to-ceiling windows. If weather permits, take advantage of the rooftop terrace with great views over Berlin—just remember to bring your own drinks, as there is no bar. Major sites like Tiergarten and the Berlin Zoo are 10 and 15 minutes by foot, respectively. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewSet in a restored 1913 Art Nouveau building along leafy Oranienplatz, Orania is one of the few hotels—and the only upscale option—in the edgy, nightlife-filled Kreuzberg. A large, open-plan "Living Room," which functions as a restaurant-bar-lounge, is bookended by two roaring fireplaces (in winter) and surrounded by enormous windows; a raised corner stage sports a Steinway piano (there's classical or jazz most nights). The rooms and suites vary in size and layout, but all are similarly designed: lots of rich woods, deep red textiles featuring the hotel’s signature gold elephant, handmade Persian carpets, and curvaceous lamps from Catellani. If you're a frequent visitor to Berlin and love nightlife, this hotel is ideal for you. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewA renovated 1950s high-rise is home to the Berlin outpost of this hip German hotel chain, which is sandwiched between the Berlin Zoo and the trendy concept mall Bikini Berlin. There's a fun energy as soon as you walk into the third-floor reception area, dubbed Bikini Island, which sports a playful jungle-themed design, with tropical plants, stuffed monkeys, and hammocks perfectly positioned to look out over the zoo’s monkey and bird cages. All rooms, even the ones called XL, are on the smaller side, but the funky Jungle Rooms, many with their own hammocks overlooking the zoo, offer an escape different from others you can find in the city. The hotel is also home to the Monkey Bar, one of Berlin's most popular cocktail spots, and guests can cut the line by taking a private elevator straight to the door. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewThis five-star property, long known for its impeccable white-glove service, has a sophisticated look that nods to 1920s Berlin. Entry-level Deluxe Rooms are plenty spacious, measuring a generous 430 square feet, but it’s worth trading up to a Deluxe View Room for fantastic views overlooking Potsdamer Platz. For even more exclusivity, the 42 Club Level rooms and suites on the 10th and 11th floors offer 24-hour access to a lounge with panoramic city vistas, complimentary food and drink, and a private concierge. The elegant sandstone tower fits right in with the neighboring skyscrapers on bustling Potsdamer Platz, and guests are a short stroll from the Holocaust Memorial, the Brandenburg Gate, and Tiergarten park's 519 acres of tree-lined paths and flowering gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewFrom the outside, the circa-1970s building housing The Hoxton doesn’t look like anything special. But step into the oversized lobby chock-full of comfy places to sit (with your choice of chairs and sectionals arranged around tables of various shapes and sizes, along with one long communal coworking table), and you see why the young (and young at heart) could spend all day here. When the mood strikes for a drink, the sophisticated bar lies right behind the lobby, separated by staggered shelves displaying artfully arranged vases, jars, books, and other design knickknacks. And since the Hoxton also has its own coffee shop (technically a teahouse) and Indian restaurant, it’s truly a place that invites lingering. Each of the 234 guest rooms has a similar look, with scalloped headboards in muted pink and green, speckled terrazzo side tables, Art Nouveau lamps, and hardwood floors. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1914 in the style of a French palace, this magnificent villa has served as a private residence, embassy, naval officers’ club, and later, a luxury hotel, hosting notable guests such as Romy Schneider and Paul McCartney. In 2014, late Berlin fashion designer Patrick Hellmann acquired the property and began renovations, restoring its glorious historical details while bringing much of the design—previously done by Karl Lagerfeld in the 1990s—firmly into the 21st century. The 43 rooms and 9 suites feature particularly impressive details: A dual-bedroom Kaiser Suite boasts an antique library with original frescoes, and the first-floor Karl Lagerfeld Suite has lovely Art Deco touches and a stone balcony overlooking the gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewVladimir Nabokov, Brigitte Bardot, and Alain Delon have all stayed at this luxury hotel at some point in its history. It opened in 1913 on a quiet, leafy square in posh Charlottenburg and was renovated a century later as part of Marriott’s Autograph Collection. It was just spruced up again in 2025 after its takeover by the Germany-based, design-focused Roomers brand. The boutique property retains its alluring Art Nouveau flourishes, including a sinuous canopy above the entrance, Moorish arched windows, and exquisite stucco work throughout. The flawless redesign integrates historic decorative elements with contemporary touches. The luxurious boutique vibe and ideal location—just a short walk to the shops along Kurfürstendamm and the Berlin Zoo—make it an enduring draw, even after the redo. —J.C. FAQ: What is the best area to stay in when visiting Berlin? For first-timers who want to get a true feel for the city, Mitte is the beating creative heart of Berlin, and where you'll find some of our favorite locally-grown hotels, including Telegraphenamt and Chateau Royal Berlin. Another ideal option is Charlottenburg, in western Berlin, which is home to upscale shopping, the grand Charlottenburg Palace, and hotels like The Hoxton. How do we choose the best hotels in Berlin? Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. item.title: The Best Luxury Cruise Lines Now Rival the Finest Hotels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.53
The luxury cruising landscape—or seascape, rather—has grown tremendously over the past few years. And it's no longer just traditional ocean cruises. Travelers accustomed to the finer things in life can now have their pick among expedition vessels plying previously inaccessible polar regions, sumptuous river ships sailing from the Amazon to the Mekong, and flashy new superyachts worthy of Page Six. Aboard, passengers can expect all the same perks they'd find at the world's most exclusive hotels, from personal butlers to multi-story penthouses. This year alone has seen a boom in ultra-luxe yachts, built not by established names in the cruising industry but rather by hotel brands. Sailing with far fewer passengers, they give the vibe more of a private charter or a floating hotel than a traditional cruise ship, with thoughtful approaches to dining and design. Scheduling, too, is shifting. Many posh lines are extending Mediterranean itineraries into the shoulder season and even winter, meaning there are more options for luxury voyages than ever before. Not to be left behind, the old guard—Regent Seven Seas Cruises, Seabourn, Crystal—are continuously making adjustments to meet the needs of today's luxury traveler. Regent is reducing the passenger count on Explorer Class ships to expand cabin sizes while readying to unveil the opulent Seven Seas Prestige ship in December. Seabourn will soon announce a fleet-wide makeover of its culinary programs. Crystal, which has dropped “Cruises” from its brand name, is readying the new-build Crystal Grace for June 2028. Luxury is also creeping aboard expedition ships. Silversea extends its all-suite, butler-outfitted, complimentary caviar philosophy to four exploration vessels, including the Galapagos-only 100-passenger Silver Origin. Scenic Luxury Cruises & Tours, now sailing two sleek 270-passenger yachts capable of polar cruising, debuts 270-passenger Scenic Ikon with two helicopters, a submersible, and 15 dining venues in April 2028. Luxe French line Ponant scores with 245-passenger Le Commandant Charcot, the only luxury icebreaker at sea and can sail to the true North Pole. Seabourn sails the 264-passenger Seabourn Venture and twin Seabourn Pursuit, two lavish all-suite polar-class expedition ships cruising remote itineraries, each with two submarines. All of this to say, there’s never been a better time to hop aboard a luxury cruise line. Below, we round up the names to know across all categories. Yacht The 94-passenger Amangati, which is now open for reservations and will set sail in spring 2027, embodies the hotel brand’s space and privacy design, and even offers a two-deck spa with a Japanese serenity garden. It’s so catered to the one-percenter that it offers “host suites” for passengers’ personal service or security staff as well as two helipads. Consider this ship particularly ripe for charter. The 95-suite, residential-leaning Four Seasons I, which debuted in March 2026, has a one-to-one passenger-crew ratio, meaning your needs will never go unmet. The 79-suite Four Seasons II will arrive in May 2028 for further Med sails, showcasing two-to-four-bedroom suites on the upper decks and a whopping 11 culinary concepts. Only breakfast is included in cruise fares, a luxury cruise first. (Passengers should plan for about $250 per day, per person for food and beverage.) Late stays and overnights in ports, deep dives into well-being (including the Lanserhof Reset, a longevity experience on the November inaugural transatlantic crossing courtesy of the renowned medi-spa group), and personalized shore excursions are among the amenities. This line’s stunning bespoke ships feature three fully automated rigs capable of delivering 100% wind-powered propulsion in favorable conditions. Dynamic positioning and LNG propulsion are among its energy-efficient and environmental accomplishments. The 54-suite Orient Express Corinthian features five restaurants under the culinary direction of superstar chef Yannick Alléno, whose restaurants have won multiple Michelin stars, and sails the Med until autumn. Twin Orient Express Olympian sets sail next spring. Some excursions are included in the price, others are not. From the hotel brand known for its luxe amenities, personalized service, and fine dining, find three all-suite, all-inclusive ships—149-suite Evrima, 224-suite Ilma, and 226-suite Luminara. Each offers five restaurants and a marina for watersports. Menus from the brand’s Michelin-star-earning chefs are de rigueur, as are personalized spa therapies, and high-end boutiques such as Cartier. Expedition Le Commandant Charcot, the only luxury icebreaker, can travel to the true North Pole and other ice-bound destinations. This French ship offers Le Nuna, the only Alain Ducasse fine-dining restaurant at sea. Ponant also features six bilingual explorer ships for warmer climes. This elegant ocean-going line sails two twin expedition ships, 264-passenger Seabourn Venture and Seabourn Pursuit. Both possess PC6 Polar Class standards, meaning they are capable of pushing through ice. All-suite accommodations, excellent dining, and crew pampering enhance expedition adventures. Scenic currently possesses two sleek 228-passenger ultra-luxury vessels dubbed “discovery yachts” excelling at polar cruising. Both feature 10 dining venues, a spacious spa, two helicopters, one submersible, Zodiacs, kayaks, and stand-up paddleboards. Beyond its classic ocean liners, Silversea’s four expedition ships include three venturing to Poles, Kimberley, Australia, and other remote locales, and one in the Galapagos. Silversea is also opening The Cormorant at 55 South, the Earth’s southernmost hotel in Puerto Williams, as an easier waystation to Antarctica, in October 2026. Ocean Crystal’s two ultra-luxurious ships, 740-passenger Crystal Serenity and 606-passenger Crystal Symphony, feature butler service for all, pillow menus, a Nobu Matsuhisa-affiliated Asian restaurant, and 24-hour room service. Owned by Abercrombie & Kent Travel Group, Abercrombie & Kent partners with Crystal for special voyages combining land elements.
