With three 922-passenger ships already sailing, EJ unveils Explora IV in summer 2027 with 461 suites, five heated pools, and seven restaurants. This ship and Explora III feature a private dining chef’s table, beach-club-style Shore Club eatery, wine-tasting cellar, and an expanded kids club with family-oriented destination experiences. Near-twin Explora V sets sail in December 2027 and Explora VI in August 2028. Oceania’s seven ships are devoted to culinary superiority. Beyond Oceania Sonata, discover Oceania Aurelia, with just 238 accommodations, in November 2027, and Oceania Arietta in 2029. Oceania Cruises teams with Condé Nast Traveler editors for insider tips on activities ashore. Bilingual French line Ponant is hailed for intriguing itineraries across 12 intimate ships, from sailing vessels to expedition. English-only cruises sail in partnerships, often with Smithsonian Journeys. The December debut of Seven Seas Prestige heralds the newest of the line's seven-ship fleet. Lavish new suite categories feature accommodations with in-suite elevators, private gyms, and personal butlers. These three ocean liners feel more quiet luxury than over-the-top opulent—just the way devotees like it. The all-suite 600-passenger Seabourn Encore and Seabourn Ovation offer multiple fine-dining venues and a fee-extra Retreat for extra privacy and service. The 458-passenger Seabourn Quest just underwent an extensive refurbishment. With two twin mega-yachts, 112-passenger SeaDream I and SeaDream II sport a relaxed yachting lifestyle. Signature elements include sophisticated cuisine, attentive crew, and a watersports marina platform. SeaDream III promises a somewhat bigger and more elevated sailing experience to more destinations in 2029. Beyond exploration vessels, Silversea sails eight all-suite ultra-luxury ships where butlers pamper passengers and complimentary caviar abounds. Expect multiple other included amenities, too. River The three all-suite ships in this European line arguably deliver the best gastronomic experiences on rivers. Included outings might range from an al fresco candlelit dinner at a French winery to private palace concerts in Vienna. Ever-expanding Uniworld will count some 24 distinctly designed ships by 2028, each reflecting the sailing region. The design-forward riverboats mirror charming boutique hotels, with itineraries in Europe, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Egypt. Not as uber-luxury as some of the other names here, AmaWaterways is a more affordable luxury river cruise option that still offers an incredible sense of intimacy and low-impact cruising thanks to the ships' small sizes. Most notable recently is the line's launch of an itinerary on Colombia's Magdalena River, the first of its kind since the days of the steam ship. With one of the most extensive fleet of river cruises vessels in the world, river cruising is Viking’s bread and butter. While Viking falls on the more accessible end of the luxury cruise spectrum, it’s frequently voted the best river cruise line in the world by CNT readers thanks to its Scandanavian design, exceptional service, Nordic spas, and adults-only atmosphere.

item.title: From Kendall Jenner to the Clooneys: This is Where the A-list Stays for the Venice Film Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.48
For over 80 years now the Venice International Film Festival has attracted the world's most glamorous and famous crowd. In the 1950s, it saw Brigitte Bardot pose for paparazzi while sitting on grass, and Elizabeth Taylor take a dip in the lido at Hotel Excelsior Venice. Fast forward to today and it's just as star-studded, with the 83rd Venice International Film Festival hosting an array of actors, supermodels and musicians, from Laura Dern to Robert Pattinson, Irina Shayk and Liam Gallagher. Much of the red carpet action takes place at Hotel Excelsior Venice, which has hosted the main event since 1932. Notably, following a three-year closure, the hotel reopened last year (2025), to reveal a grand renovation and thus many of this year's attendees – Kate Mara, Claire Foy, Maggie Gyllenhaal – have also chosen to stay in the boldly striped suites. It's not the only top hotel in Venice that is known to host film festival attendees. The A-listers that prefer something more private often book into one of the 24 opulent rooms within Aman Venice – not only do the Clooneys love to stay here, they also married in the Palazzo Papadopoli location in 2014. To be even further removed and escape the flashes of paparazzi, Hotel Cipriani, A Belmond Hotel, Venice sits on the eastern tip of the Giudecca island. Its peaceful location has been a long- time favourite for the world's most famous stars, with previous guests including Sophia Loren, Cary Grant, and more recently Jennifer Lawrence and Lady Gaga.

item.title: The Best Airbnbs, Lodges, and Hotels Near Carlsbad Caverns National Park
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.30
Home to jaw-dropping cave formations that look like something out of an H.R. Giger painting, Carlsbad Caverns National Park is hands down one of the most spectacular cave systems in the world. Here, travelers can marvel at jellyfish-shaped rock towers, embark on ranger-guided tours into the caves’ darkest depths, and stand in awe (as I did, for the first time at age nine) as hundreds of thousands of bats emerge to feast on flying insects each evening. However, getting to this remote desert cavern is no picnic—travelers typically road trip to the tiny town of Carlsbad or fly through El Paso to witness these underground wonders. As such, lodging in the area is limited, and finding the right place to bed down after a day of adventure can be a tricky feat, even if you’ve been visiting the park for decades, like me. To find the best of the best, I spoke to park experts and scoured the web for the ultimate vacation rentals, lodges, and hotels near Carlsbad Caverns for your next stay. If you’re looking for an adorable tiny house, a riverside home for the whole crew, or a family-friendly hotel stay, you’re in the right place. How to plan a trip to Carlsbad Caverns National Park How do you get to Carlsbad Caverns? Carlsbad Caverns National Park sits about 20 miles southwest of the town of Carlsbad, New Mexico, via Highway 62/180. Due to the park’s remote location but close proximity to the highway, most travelers opt to road trip. If you're flying in, El Paso International Airport is your best bet, set roughly two hours southwest by car. Nearby, Guadalupe Mountains and White Sands national parks are within a day’s drive, making for an easy three-park combo for the park completionists among us, like yours truly. When is the best time of year to go to Carlsbad Caverns? One thing that I love about cave parks: the interior temperature of the caverns stays the same year-round. This makes Carlsbad Caverns an amazing national park during shoulder season (spring and fall) and winter, when others are covered in snow or inaccessible. Pack a light hoodie and expect a constant 56°F climate inside the caves. Hoping to catch the bat flight program? Head to the park in August or September, when baby bats join hundreds of thousands of adults on their nightly quest to find food.

item.title: The Most Beautiful National Parks in Canada, From the Tourist Favorites to the Hidden Gems
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.30
From the peaks of the Canadian Rockies to the deep woods of northern Ontario to the prairies where bison still roam, Canada’s national parks span some seriously beautiful and ecologically important terrain. Since I moved to the Great White North more than 20 years ago, I’ve wanted to visit all of the country’s protected areas—and I’m now about halfway through the country's 37 national parks and 11 national park reserves. Some of Canada's most stunning parks are well-known, like Banff National Park, where turquoise lakes, natural hot springs, and miles of mountain hiking trails draw more than four million visitors each year. Others, like Auyuittuq National Park in Nunavut’s Arctic wilderness, or Mingan Archipelago National Park Reserve in northeastern Quebec, are harder to reach and less trodden—but just as gobsmacking. Below, I’ve spotlighted 11 of the most beautiful national parks in Canada, from coast to coast, to inspire your own travel wish list. See what speaks to you, and I'll see you on the trails!

item.title: 16 Best Resorts on Private Islands for an Ultra-Exclusive Getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.22
For many, true relaxation looks like dropping off the map—settling down on a secluded, sparsely populated island where no one knows anything about you, save for your favorite tropical cocktail. The very best private island resorts balance downtime and adventure; personal space and hospitality; rugged, natural beauty and state-of-the-art facilities. Scattered across the turquoise waters of Indonesia, the Maldives, and Turks and Caicos, some of these properties are wonderfully far-flung, while others, like Little Palm Island Resort & Spa in Florida and Lovango Resort and Beach Club in the US Virgin Islands, don’t even require a US passport. No matter where you decide to book your bungalow, you can rest assured that exclusivity and quietude take top priority at the properties on this list. Offering everything from fresh meals tailored to your preferences to bespoke spa treatments, these resorts are built on the idea that it’s all for you. Whether you’re seeking an open-air villa that floats above crystal-clear water, a luxury ecolodge powered by wind turbines, or a safari-style escape where jungle hikes are always on the table, these are the world’s best private island resorts—each the very definition of paradise. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tetiaroa, French Polynesia Actor Marlon Brando’s legacy lives on at his former private getaway in French Polynesia, now a hyper-exclusive, eco-minded retreat where travelers come to escape it all. Relax in one of 35 stylish, palm-thatched villas, each a grand fusion of indoor and outdoor space, the beach just footsteps away (alternatively, go even bigger with the island’s sole over-the-top residence). Enjoy island bike rides, treatments in the stickwork cocoons of the Varua te Ora Polynesian Spa, and French-tinged, Polynesian-influenced dining by French celebrity chef Jean Imbert. Nature tours led by in-house researchers offer a deeper connection to the island, while daily cultural experiences like Polynesian dance classes, ukulele lessons, and traditional weaving sessions introduce guests to local traditions. Make sure to save time to explore the other islands of the Tetiaroa Atoll, which also belong to the Brando family, where untouched beaches, preserved reefs, and thriving seabird colonies are as gorgeous as when Brando first encountered the location in 1960. All meals, libations (including Champagne), in-room dining, and daily spa treatments are bundled into the all-inclusive rate, allowing for carefree indulgence at every turn. And although The Brando immerses guests in barefoot ultra-luxury, it also quietly stands as one of the world’s most sustainable resorts—powered by solar energy and cooled by innovative seawater systems—preserving the paradise Brando so deeply loved for generations to come. —Antonia Quirke - Read Full ReviewLocation: Little Torch Key, Florida This adults-only private island is a study in tropical chic, redefining the castaway fantasy right on American soil. There are a total of 30 thatched-roof bungalow suites (some freestanding, some within larger bungalows) across the four-acre island, many with four-poster beds and outdoor copper bathtubs. Thanks to a smart layout and smarter landscaping, you’ll encounter other people less often than you’d expect (a strict cap at 60 guests helps). All suites have water views, outdoor showers, and furnished decks; most also overlook private slivers of white-sand beach and are kitted out with hammocks, loungers, and firepits. The Dining Room has sweeping sea views, and the spectacular SpaTerre complex is underscored by a breezy two-story atrium. Paddleboard or kayak through mangrove mazes as eagle rays swim by, laze the day away on a beachfront hammock, or simply enjoy the day resting on a poolside lounger. Also, don’t miss a snorkeling trip to Looe Key Reef, part of the third-largest living coral reef in the world and site of ongoing reef restoration efforts by MOTE Marine Laboratory & Aquarium, a Florida-based nonprofit marine research institution. Little Palm Island has partnered with the organization to create the “Paradise with a Purpose” package, which includes a half-day in Looe Key Reef, a donation to MOTE Marine, accommodations, and breakfast. —Paul Rubio - Read Full ReviewLocation: Yaukuve Levu Island, Fiji Located in the untouched Kadavu Islands, a 45-minute seaplane flight from Nadi International Airport, this private island balances romance and multigenerational travel in Fiji. Straddling the renowned Great Astrolabe Reef, the waters near Kokomo teem with colorful fish, manta rays, sea turtles, and thriving coral gardens, making underwater exploration a must for any visit (don’t miss the marine biologist–led manta snorkel excursion). Twenty-one beachfront villas range in size from a couples-friendly one-bedroom to larger two- and three-bedrooms, each with a private plunge pool, private walled garden with outdoor shower, and direct beach access. Meanwhile, five hilltop luxury Grand Residences welcome larger families to multi-bedroom homes, inclusive of a private butler and nanny. Guests can also anticipate other water activities like sailing and kayaking, and three memorable meals daily, made of locally sourced produce from Kokomo’s 5.5-acre farm and hydroponics garden, and seafood from a sustainable, caught-to-order island initiative. —Adam H. Graham - Read Full ReviewLocation: Anambas, Indonesia There are drop-dead gorgeous private island resorts, and then there’s Bawah, an entire nature and marine reserve comprising 6 islands, 3 blue lagoons, and 13 unspoiled white beaches in the heart of Indonesia’s Anambas Archipelago. Sustainability lies at the core of the reserve with no compromises on luxury. In fact, the entire resort was constructed by hand using sustainable bamboo and locally sourced natural building materials, and decorated with works from local artisans. The reserve oozes natural splendor, which can be enjoyed from the comfort of a swoon-worthy rustic-chic tented suite, overwater bungalow, or pool villa. Come here for Indonesian coastal cuisine perfected, dinners in the treetops, spectacular sunsets, hikes through the jungle, island-hopping via transparent kayaks, and sublime snorkeling. To access Bawah’s remote location with ease, the reserve offers a door-to-door transfer from Singapore airport with short components by road and ferry, followed by a 75-minute seaplane that lands directly in paradise. —Michelle Jana Chan - Read Full ReviewLocation: Peter Island, British Virgin Islands From the moment the resort’s yacht glides into the serene waters of Yacht Harbor in Sprat Bay, the transition from passenger to prized guest is practically instantaneous. Peter Island, the largest private island in the British Virgin Islands, turns up the volume on the wellness-minded, pastoral strains of Caribbean life, and in no time, you might just find yourself humming along to the tune. With just 52 rooms and 2 villas, you’ll never have to battle for privacy and discretion, yet the company of fellow guests is always welcome. In 2017, Hurricane Irma tragically destroyed homes and upended lives throughout the Virgin Islands. The resort strives to be as sustainable as possible; it has a reverse osmosis water purification plant and two wind turbines that can generate up to 75% of the island's power. And yet Peter Island still doesn't mess with what works, and leans into a familial flavor of hospitality that feels like you’re at your favorite aunt and uncle’s for the holidays. —Kat Chen - Read Full ReviewLocation: Mnemba Island, Tanzania Just shy of two miles off the coast of Zanzibar’s main island, Mnemba is a tiny, casuarina-forested sanctuary surrounded by a private marine reserve. Home to just 12 shell-shaped, thatched bandas, designed with understated elegance by Fox Browne Creative and Jack Alexander Studio, it’s the antithesis of bling. A seven-month rebuild in 2024 expanded the villas into curvaceous, nautilus-like spaces, blending natural materials with breezy open-air design. Guests can explore turquoise shallows on catamarans, dive vibrant reefs, or simply lounge in private beach bandas watching noddies and plovers whirl above the sandspit. The spa, yoga deck, and Oceans Without Borders education center enrich the experience, while chefs curate custom menus that range from sushi boxes to lobster ravioli served under the stars. Service is impeccable, with a charming butler, a jovial bar team, and Tanzania’s first local dive master leading ocean explorations. Despite Zanzibar’s tourism boom, Mnemba feels like a world apart—exclusive, untouched, and deeply serene. With a staff-to-guest ratio of over 3:1, every detail is handled, leaving you to do exactly what you’re meant to here: absolutely nothing. —Lisa Grainger - Read Full ReviewLocation: Nosy Ankao, Madagascar A nothing-is-impossible hideaway for adventurous high-fliers, Miavana by Time + Tide is set on remote Nosy Ankao in northern Madagascar, only reachable by helicopter. With ease, the private island merges barefoot luxury and a deep commitment to conservation and community support. Just 14 villas, built from sun-bleached Malagasy wood and hand-hewn limestone, sprawl across private gardens and powder-soft beaches. Interiors channel a beachy Palm Springs vibe, with sunken bathtubs, pastel Smeg appliances, and fully stocked kitchens, offering a luxurious home-away-from-home feeling. The central Piazza serves farm-fresh menus that change daily, while off-menu requests are happily fulfilled. Though there’s no stand-alone spa, therapists deliver seashell massages and herbal body wraps directly to your villa. Service is breezy yet impeccable, with butlers anticipating every need—whether folding laundry, crafting green juices, or lending sunglasses. Miavana by Time + Tide’s eco-efforts are serious: villas rely on natural ventilation, solar panels power much of the resort, and local conservation programs protect turtles, lemurs, and coral reefs. While private island life is great, take time to explore mainland Madagascar’s iconic baobab forests or Tsingy formations (both can be arranged by helicopter safari from the island). —Chris Schalkx - Read Full ReviewLocation: Islas Secas, Panama Set within the jungle-cloaked splendor of Panama’s Gulf of Chiriquí, Islas Secas offers an exclusive, eco-friendly escape across a private archipelago of 14 untouched islands. At its heart, the resort’s eight light-footed accommodations—including casitas, safari-style tents, and open-air mansion Casa Cavada—blend flawlessly into the landscape, each with sweeping hilltop views and living spaces that celebrate the outdoors. Guests have exclusive access to this entire island chain, blanketed in tropical flora and fringed by white- and gold-sand beaches. Days unfold as you please across the various islands: kayak through emerald waters, snorkel vibrant coral gardens, hike jungle trails to ancient artifacts, or island-hop to wide, sparkling beaches where staff can arrange private beach barbecues. Water adventures abound, too, from fun on pricey water toys like hydrofoils, flyboards, and Seabobs, to fishing and whale-watching, all included in the resort’s personalized, all-inclusive program. On the main island of Isla Cavada, find a stunning open-air beachfront restaurant, a swoon-worthy jungle spa, a Hemingway-inspired bar, and an infinity pool perched high above the rainforest coastline. —Andrea Whittle - Read Full ReviewLocation: Necker Island, British Virgin Islands Necker Island is the creation of Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson, who has transformed what was once a scrubby, 74-acre British Virgin Island cay into a fortress of lush greenery, serene Balinese villas, exotic animals ranging from local flamingos to endangered lemurs and tortoises, and solar panels and wind turbines that make the island self-sustaining. The resort is accessible only by boat from nearby Tortola—no private-plane runway here—which makes it feel more approachable and refuge-like, especially compared to some other private-island hospitality projects. Every inch of the place feels like a Bond hideaway: Tropical canopies give way to white-sand beaches all your own, lagoons filled with flamingos, infinity-pooled suites, and cozy lounges. A sprawling hilltop Great House has far-flung views of the azure waters around the island; there's also a billiards table, board games, a bar (just one of many on the island, including the self-serve one in your own villa), and dining nooks with incredible views where five-star, family-style dinners and healthy à la carte breakfasts are served. —Shannon McMahon - Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos Located off the main chain of Turks and Caicos, Ambergris Cay achieves billionaire-level relaxation with its serene azure waters, rugged nature, and waterfront villas. The 1,100-acre island is home to a collection of expansive villas, from 1-bedroom beachfront bungalows to 10-bedroom homes. All meals and house beverages are included, meaning you’ll never go hungry—or thirsty—with cocktails made from fresh ingredients and a floating rum bar called The Hangover accessible only by boat. Suites sit on the sugar-sand beach leading into the Caribbean Sea, while sprawling villas are perched on craggy hilltops overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. Interiors are beach house chic, with wood-plank floors and shiplap walls. Guests roam the island via golf cart between the spa, tennis courts, beach activities, and state-of-the-art fitness center encased in 180 degrees of glass. Service is breezy but attentive, with 24/7 concierge support via WhatsApp. The private island resort also houses one of the longest runways in the region, making it easy for outdoor-minded billionaires and professional athletes to arrive in private jets for instant immersion into the tropical good life. —S.M. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lovango Cay, US Virgin Islands Located across St. John’s legendary Caneel Bay on an island all its own, this unpretentious seasonal resort (open December through July) features the USVI’s only private island beach club and eco-chic accommodation in the form of wooden treehouses, explorer-style tents, and one- to three-bedroom villas. Views of the surrounding jewel-toned waters abound, peaking at Treetops Lobby Tent, where bird's-eye views of St. John proper and St. Thomas can be admired in a single panorama. Indulge in island cuisine and rum-spiked fun at the resort’s Waterfront Restaurant (get the smoked pineapple old- fashioned and the signature Caribbean lobster paillard) or its fast-casual counterpart, Sand Pit, which services Lovango’s Beach Club and its cabana-lined swimming pool. For active and gastronomic pursuits in greater St. John, take the ferry to Cruz Bay, which runs regularly; for another incarnation of beach bliss, hop on the five-minute ferry to St. John’s Honeymoon Beach, which runs on select days. —Todd Plummer - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lhaviyani Atoll, Maldives This Yuji Yamazaki–designed property in the Maldives’s Lhaviyani Atoll is a next-generation ultra-luxury experience like no other, underscored by a mind-blowing “Anything, Anytime, Anywhere” fixed price policy, where few things are off-limits—nor cost extra—from floating breakfasts to most top-shelf Champagne to private fitness training. The island’s 15 ryokan-inspired overwater residences epitomize contemporary Japanese ocean elegance, offering ample room to relax and play against the backdrop of the Maldives’ lazuline beauty (units start at 3,300 square feet). At Kudadoo’s core lies The Retreat, an impressive open-air minimalist overwater pagoda crowned by 984 solar panels (that power the resort in its entirety) and housing the island’s bar, restaurant, spa, fitness facilities, and lounge areas. Thanks to the Anything, Anytime, Anywhere policy, your residence, The Retreat, and the surrounding nature become your muses for fulfilling the utmost island fantasies. Request to be marooned on nearby Dream Island for a luxury-draped Robinson Crusoe experience or ask for a private toes-in-the-sand beach lunch on Kudadoo itself. Snorkel with giant mantas alongside a marine biologist or try your hand at jet-skiing, parasailing, or fishing. Pencil in plenty of time for spa treatments—they are unlimited, after all—before or after you figure out how to manage an entire staff of butlers, cooks, personal trainers, and yoga masters at your beck and call. Suffice to say, Kudadoo is the ultimate castaway narrative come to life—and the script is yours to write. —L.G. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Moskito Island, British Virgin Islands While everyone knows about billionaire Richard Branson’s original private retreat, Necker Island, the Virgin founder purchased another exclusive playground just two miles away called Moskito Island. But instead of using it for himself and his high-powered pals, the mogul built a home and sold nine other plots for others to build their dream beach houses. While most are only inhabited by the estate owners themselves, three of the remarkable properties—The Branson Estate, The Oasis Estate, and The Point Estate—became available for rent in October 2021. Although more expensive than your average luxury hotel, Moskito Island makes living the life of a billionaire a tiny bit more accessible. Five-star restaurants are swapped for private chefs, hotel suites for exclusive estates, and concierges for dedicated house managers capable of making nearly anything you want possible. The only guests in sight are those in your immediate party—that is, unless you decide to venture to the communal Manchioneel Beach, complete with a floating trampoline and bartenders at the ready, or the Beach House, a community recreational area where you can play a round of tennis and mingle with estate owners (you may even spot Richard Branson himself). —Jordi Lippe-McGraw - Gold List 2018, 2019, 2020Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos As COMO’s sole property in the Americas, Parrot Cay's renowned luxury experience makes it an unrivaled property in Turks and Caicos. The pinnacle of bespoke solitude, it's located on a private island enmeshed in the wilderness. You arrive after a 15-minute chauffeured drive from Providenciales International Airport, then a 20-minute panoramic boat ride through cays and turquoise waves hugged by mangroves. It’s primeval in nature and worlds away, despite its ease of access from the main island. The private, white-sand beach—with miles of clear-water sandbars inviting you to walk across, float around, and laze about for ages—is the main reason why the property has been dubbed by locals as "the Maldives of the Americas," despite being entirely singular in the impression it makes. If you’re seeking a romantic getaway inspired by an itch for an immersive nature escape, this is the place to go—and I recommend booking a private beach house with your own plunge pool for the full immersive experience. —Bridget Knowles FAQ: How we choose the best private island resorts in the world Every resort on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: The Last-Chance Tourism of Iceland's Glacier Raves
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.08
Weaving through the crowd, I pause next to Kali Van Horn, a 30-year-old architect from Brooklyn with glitter dripping from her eyes like crystallized tears. We share the moment as strangers, pressing our backs against the frozen wall as two DJs spin house and techno tracks in the heart of Langjökull—Iceland’s second-largest glacier. “It’s healing,” Van Horn says, as rainbow lights illuminate the ice cave’s blue hues. Surrounding us are people wearing winter coats accessorized with light-up scarves, sparkly snowflake-shaped sunglasses, and hoods lined with lavender fur. This is part of Iceland Eclipse, a festival on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, offering late-night raves, cacao ceremonies, and lectures on whale communication to 3,333 total attendees. There’s a strong Burning Man overlap among the crowd, from longtime Burners to attendees drawn to the festival’s mix of music, spirituality, and spectacle. Most are here to extend their experience of the total solar eclipse one day prior, for which they’ve traveled great distances and invested even more grandly. This experience, an 11-hour, $600-price-tagged excursion called “Into the Glacier”, is perhaps the most exclusive event on the lineup. More than ever, rare natural wonders and phenomena are gaining top billing for luxury travel experiences—and this one, both in ambition and vibe, is a standout, drawing just 100 attendees to commune with this 395 square-mile mass of ice. As we drive from the festival grounds toward Langjökull, the stark landscape is punctuated by the occasional sprig of purple flowers. Spikes jut from the massive tires of our car—a vehicle bearing a Jägermeister sticker and the license plate JAGER—which crunches over gravel as the Red Hot Chili Peppers blasts through the speakers, and ravers in the back seat discuss ketamine and the rise of AI. The cars climb higher on the glacier until they begin to get stuck. Then, when they inevitably do, drivers jump out and release air from the tires, redistributing weight so they can continue. The rocks around us fade into sheets of textured ice as we drive onto the glacier, streams of clear water rushing through jagged indentations. This glacier is thousands of years old, our driver explains, formed from layer after layer of snow compressing into ice. As we exit the vehicle, I notice an entrance in the ice—a portal beckoning us to another dimension. We enter the passage, its walls carved entirely from the glacier. I’m still dangling my crampon—a spiked traction device for walking on slippery ice—in one hand when an Into the Glacier staff member swoops in, gliding it over my hiking shoe in a single fluid motion. “Cinderella treatment,” he says with a grin. I follow a faint beat as I meander through a 1,640-foot labyrinth—the largest manmade ice tunnel in the world—before stepping into a wider, taller space within the ice. It’s designed like a chapel, with wooden benches and faux flowers forming a heart on the wall. Near the exit stands a bearded Into the Glacier tour guide whose name is Hjalamroli Hjalmrsson, I learn, and who tells me his age is “young and old at the same time.” We’re lucky to be partying in the Icelandic Highlands, he impresses upon me: 1,300 meters above sea level, surrounded by “500 billion tons of snow, water, and ice.” The sound dances around us. “It's very echoey. You feel the bass is bouncing off the icy walls,” Hjalmrsson says. “The sound kind of drowns, but that's interesting. It's something that you can compare to a big warehouse.” Just two days ago, when I met with Iceland Eclipse’s co-producer Fridrik Olafsson, 41, he told me that he chose not to haul up large amounts of audio or lighting equipment for the event—“the setting itself does the trick,” he said, spreading his hands on the table. His wife had stenciled a drawing of a moon embracing the sun on his thumbnail. On his other hand, a crescent moon with a face howled. Olafsson took a phone call four minutes into our interview, speaking in terse Icelandic, before telling me that three days of storms had ravaged the festival, damaging three main-stage tents, and ruining 50 glamping tents. He described roaring gusts of nearly 70 miles per hour, desperately tying down tents with heavy machinery, and crew members working for 24 hours to make repairs. “Us Icelanders would call it a windy day, but our foreign counterparts were absolutely shocked,” Olafsson said. Olfasson received permission from local authorities and the mayor for Iceland Eclipse excursions. He had previously collaborated with Into the Glacier—which offers daily tours inside Langjökull—while organizing a music event for Secret Solstice, an Icelandic festival he founded that ran from 2014 to 2019 and offered $1 million ticket packages for groups of six guests, including private jet rides and a personal chef. This post-eclipse event is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to upscale glacial experiences. Inside Langjökull, I follow the steady pulse of music to a mass of 100 people swaying in a hypnotic trance. Hólmar Thor Filipsson, 52, an Icelandic DJ known as Hólmar (Acid Tourist), is playing back-to-back with Margeir Steinar Ingólfsson, 51, an Icelandic DJ known as Margeir. “Everyone there was experiencing something for the first time ever,” Thor Filipsson tells me, later, back at the camp. “It was like the eclipse in a way, but more concentrated, and it felt a little bit sci-fi.” Ingólfsson operates on the same wavelength. “I even came with a special gift for the glacier from my friend, who is a glacier specialist,” Ingólfsson, 51, says. His friend has collected water from glaciers around the world, and Ingólfsson placed a few drops near the DJ booth. When I ask about the night's song selection, Ingólfsson says they took their cue from the glacier itself. Was the glacier in the mood for house and techno, I ask? “Yes,” Ingólfsson replies. “That was the vibe that the glacier wanted at this time.” As the rave beats on, cans of pink vodka cocktails appear in our gloved hands. The beverage packaging suggests that “Flamingo” is an adequate description for a flavor—apparently, that means something like the nostalgic taste of liquified pink Starbursts. Iceland Eclipse staff members are on task with collecting trash in plastic bags, the goal being to leave the glacier just as it was found. Hours later, our two-drink-maximums met, we exit the glacier and totter down to the Into the Glacier Klaki Base Camp, about 10 minutes from the ice cave’s entrance. I meet Lyndsay Klebba, a 36-year-old writer from Chicago, who is wearing a fluffy yellow hat and a pashmina decorated with spotted mushrooms. She decided to visit Iceland after a 23andMe test revealed her Viking heritage: “To be surrounded by ancient ice and listening to New Age music—it's just a clash of titans,” she says. She spent most of the party tucked behind the DJ booth, her heart against the ice to feel the bass. She also wandered into an icy alcove and stuck out her tongue to catch droplets trickling from the ceiling. “The freshest water I ever tasted.” Klebba is the exact audience that Iceland Eclipse is after—those moved by the specialness of the glacier as a setting. “Ice holds a lot of history,” says Mitch Morales, CEO of IMXP and founder of Iceland Eclipse. “The ice in the glacier is thousands of years old–I think about what was happening in the world when this ice was frozen, all the memory, and thinking about this as being a temple in the same way." Morales, 41, is planning IMXP’s “Eclipse Trilogy” of annual totality events. Just last month, he was scouting for the ideal 2027 Luxor site; he is considering Australia or New Zealand for 2028. His ambitions extend even further, though, he says: He eventually wants to host an eclipse viewing on the moon. “In Egypt, there are stone temples that are dedicated to the things that came before them. In a way, I think that a glacier party is similar to that,” Morales says. Gazing out the window as the car crept down the glacier, Klebba observes small signs showing how far Langjökull’s ice once extended. The glacier has lost an estimated 29 percent of its mass between 1890 and 2019, according to a 2020 study published in Frontiers in Earth Science. “Where we were right now would have been glacier probably 40 years ago,” Klebba says. “The fact that we had to drive up several miles just to get to it makes you think about what's going on today.” Some travelers seek out landscapes threatened by global warming, a phenomenon known as “last-chance tourism.” Langjökull has already outlived nearby Okjökull, which became Iceland’s first glacier lost to climate change in 2014. Its name was shortened to Ok, dropping jökull—Icelandic for glacier. “Knowing that this was the last chance to party inside a glacier because of climate change was a big factor in me deciding to attend,” says Hayley Sharkey, 27, reflecting on the event. Sharkey is a Miami public relations coordinator who has adorned her blue snow jacket with faux-fur cuffs. “Future generations will not be able to understand how it felt to be inside a glacier. The feeling of natural ice surrounding you will be seen as a myth.”

item.title: How to stay at the real life 'Sterling Point' cottage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.68
It’s been quite the year for TV shows and movies both set and filmed in destinations that have captured our attention and tempted us to hop on set-jetting adventures. Among the shows that have truly captured our wanderlust is Sterling Point, the young adult Prime series that follows Annie (played by Ella Rubin) and her brother Connor (Keen Ruffalo) as they unexpectedly find themselves in possession of a remote island in Ontario’s Muskoka region. Aware of their late mother’s love for the area, but taken aback by the unlikely situation they find themselves in following the passing of a grandfather they were unaware existed, Annie travels north from her hometown to experience a Canadian summer and seek answers. The series shines a spotlight on Muskoka’s breathtaking scenery and natural beauty, but there’s one question that many fans of the series were left wondering: is Sterling Point's Gordon’s Cottage a real place, and is it possible to stay there? Up until now, despite plenty of sleuthing from entertainment and travel insiders, it wasn’t possible. However, that’s set to change as the historic cottage country retreat that became an unexpected summer star is landing on Airbnb. In response to unprecedented travel demand, with searches from outside Canada for check-ins through November 2026 up almost 110 per cent year on year, the cottage is opening up to jet-jetters for just three special stays. The cottage first opened in 1902 as a summer hotel, with travellers captivated by its lakeside charm and position among the towering trees. Now, a few lucky holidaymakers will find themselves plunging into the water off the dock, sharing long meals on the 800-square-foot screened porch, and keeping an eye out for local wildlife such as loons and chipmunks. Other highlights include watching blazing sunsets that turn into spectacularly starry nights thanks to the clear Muskoka sky, morning yoga sessions and plenty of opportunities for curious guests keen to kayak, canoe and paddleboard their way around the lake. Guests can book one of three special stays between 2 - 5 October, 9 - 12 October and 16 - 19 October as of 9am ET (12pm GMT) on 15 September at a cost of $180 CAD (£96) per night.

item.title: UK airport latest: thousands of flights delayed and cancelled at UK airports
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.40
Several major UK airports are continuing to experience delays and cancellations following a major air traffic control technical failure on Tuesday 8 September. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption is expected to continue into Wednesday as airlines and airports work through the backlog. NATs boss Martin Rolfe has apologised for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped". An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before travelling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” FlightRadar24 is currently reporting that 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday 9 September have already been cancelled, with the vast majority at Heathrow, while further delays and cancellations are expected as aircraft and crew displaced by Tuesday's disruption are repositioned. Passengers should check the status of their flight directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruption include: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport Can I get a refund if my flight was disrupted? If your flight was delayed or cancelled following Tuesday’s air traffic control issues at NATS, you may be entitled to flight compensation. According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, passengers can claim compensation ranging from £220 per person to £520 per person if the delay causes you to reach your destination airport more than three hours late. If the delay is more than five hours, you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Because air traffic control issues are typically considered “extraordinary circumstances” outside the airline's control, cash payouts aren't likely in this scenario. However, many airlines will still provide food and drink vouchers, airport transfers, and hotel accommodations for overnight delays. If your flight is cancelled, the airline is required to provide an alternate flight or full refund. Flight delay compensation in the UK is not automatic, and the procedure for submitting a claim varies by airline. Because the UK is no longer part of the European Union, EU passenger rights only apply to UK flights if it arrives in an EU country and is operated by an EU airline (for example, if you were flying from London to Paris with Air France). Passengers should check the status of their flight and compensation policies directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates.

item.title: In London, artisans are keeping hands-on heritage alive – meet the makers championing the craft revival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.36
There was a moment last year when the penny dropped for Guy Salter, founder of London Craft Week, a citywide celebration of the handmade that marked its 12th edition this May with nearly a quarter of a million visitors. Seeing queues amassing outside the eclectic shows, workshops, installations and talks, he thought to himself, craft is officially a thing. When Salter started the now cult event in 2015, the revival of making was already well underway, but the momentum and proliferation of craft-based practices has mushroomed across London in the decade since. In the face of an increasingly automated, AI-generated world, we are seeking objects that are human, with provenance and a sense of place. Beyond London Craft Week, the Crafts Council’s annual fair for contemporary craft and design, Collect, gathers 300 artists and makers at Somerset House each February, and organisations such as Qest (Queen Elizabeth Scholarship Trust), Cockpit Arts, The King’s Foundation and Heritage Crafts robustly support craftspeople with education, training and awareness. The craft boom has inspired amateurs too: pottery now has a primetime TV show, and basketry and textile weaving are enjoying a widespread revival – the former is celebrated at annual summer festival Tear Up. London’s craft heritage has deep roots stretching back to the 12th century, when artisans and merchants founded guilds to protect their craft and commercial interests. Groups formed for tailoring, furniture making, pewtering and dyeing, and as they got more powerful they built livery halls – in 1515 a hierarchy was introduced, including special recognition for the 12 most powerful guilds. Today 114 worshipful companies remain. Most studios are part of an intricate network of suppliers, complementary trades and outsourced workers, with London particularly well placed to support these connections, as well as provide local, national and international clients with easy access to the myriad makers tucked away in all corners of the city. Creating a new generation of craftspeople is one of the key challenges for the sector. But at a time when arts education is being relentlessly cut in schools, many companies, including the Goldsmiths’ Company and Cordwainers’ Company, actively support apprenticeships and training for their specialisms. “The opportunities for the youngsters into those trades are ever shrinking, and there’s definitely an appetite to create something where there are clearer pathways,” says shoemaker Deborah Carré. “We need to value this time and training, so it becomes part of our economic future. Living heritage is an evolving thing, not a static museum piece.” Clare Coulson Allyson Williams, seamstress Deep in the Yaa Centre, a buzzing arts hub that nurtures the creativity behind the Notting Hill Carnival through costume-making workshops, steel band studios and a central atrium for performances, is the HQ of Allyson Williams, the festival’s matriarch. Williams is lead seamstress at Genesis, one of the UK’s longest-running mas, or masquerade, bands: the collectives whose handcrafted costumes bring the traditions and stories of Afro-Caribbean ancestry and spirit – plus a contagious joy – to west London’s streets each August. The lush, syncopated rhythms of calypso music fill the air, and atelier-style cutting tables bestride deep plastic containers scarcely repressing explosions of sequins, velvet, silk, brocades and Lycra (“I’ve used every material known to man”). Shelves hold fragments of outrageously bejewelled body sculptures. It’s a fashion collection for street theatre; every year Williams creates samples referencing a theme for revellers to order from, and garments are then tailored to their specifications. Some involve wild proportions: one client masquerades as a Moko Jumbie (stilt-walking dancer). Since she established Genesis in 1980 with her late husband and Carnival co-founder, Vernon Williams, their faithful recreations of historical events and civilisations have been superseded, post-noughties, by fantastical themes rendered in meticulously decorated bodysuits. “Learning those techniques was incredibly uplifting, and exacting; there’s nowhere to hide. I’d like to be remembered as the person who brought amazing designs to life…. and made a mean bikini.” Katie Baron Anderson & Sheppard, tailors To step into the high-ceilinged, wood-panelled bespoke tailoring house of Anderson & Sheppard, established 1906, is to take a near-quantum leap into a living slice of quintessential British heritage. It’s wholeheartedly styled like a traditional gentlemen’s club, with a leather sofa, fireplace, crystal decanter and tumblers. Biblically weathered order and measurements books – tantamount to classified documents, in which every client’s details are logged by hand – line upper shelves. “We’re sticklers for tradition,” says front-of-house custodian Martin Crawford. “People like to come in and see their grandfather’s handwriting.” A corridor provides glimpses of the cutters at work, in full suiting, and paper patterns – anatomical blueprints – hanging from metal hooks. The cutters, of whom A&S has trouser and coat specialists, are essentially the architects of the design, measuring, drafting and hand cutting garments ready for construction. Here making a suit is an art form and a vocation, and the experience of buying one is aptly theatrical. A&S developed the “English drape” in the late 1920s: a softer, demilitarised, more glamorous tailoring language made for movement. Popularised by King Edward VIII, it has drawn fans in both business and the arts – including Fred Astaire and Brad Pitt. While men’s styles remain its mainstay (“Other houses are far better at suiting the female form,” says Crawford), A&S also crafted Marlene Dietrich’s famous black tux. Fluidity rules in this perfectionist’s paradise: “The job necessitates being very self-critical,” says senior cutter Leon Powell, “but our work is rooted in feeling, the ‘rock of eye’ [a tailor’s intuition].” KB Ella Merriman, rush basketry artist Cradled among the silk dyers and ceramicists of the labyrinthine Cockpit Arts building in Bloomsbury sits the studio of Ella Merriman, whose experimental twists on traditional basketry have propelled her to the forefront of the conceptual handicraft movement. Eight-foot bolts of rushes, harvested once annually in Somerset and Oxford, and bound with colourful string, line windows garlanded by chains of rush-end offcuts. Prototype works range from vessels to vast circular lighting fixtures. Her métier often involves teasing rush into unfathomably shaped objects using “weird moulds” as diverse as traffic cones and charity shop vases. Merriman works the harvested stems, dried slowly and then dampened to retain their flexibility (thick stems serve as uprights, narrower stalks the weft “threads”), around these structural bases, weaving intuitively by hand. Chairs and footstools in bright pink and yellow rest on dust-sheeted tables. The delightfully dishevelled studio echoes the poetic idiosyncrasies of nature that are central to her work and her feeling that “slight wonkiness is so beautifully human”. Regularity is anathema to Merriman’s practice, which she discovered accidentally via a short course after studying furniture and product design, and a close call with the “too rigid” world of architecture. “It felt like a remembering, rather than a learning. Working with a material like this is a relationship. In design, you’re trained to find repeatable functions, but here every stem is different and must be respected.” KB Lock & Co, hatters “We say that we make heirlooms,” says hatter Awon Golding as she stands in the tiny attic workroom on the top floor of Lock & Co Hatters’ storied shop in St James’s, where the rafters are filled with fedoras and trilbies, and artisans stitch, sculpt and trim summer’s most extravagant headwear. Celebrating its 350th anniversary this year, Lock & Co is the oldest shop in London – and the oldest hat shop in the world – yet very little about the craft has changed in that time. Hats are still made on wooden blocks (carved by Boon and Lane in Luton) and boaters are created with strip straw (where a continuous length of woven straw is handsewn in a spiral), both critically endangered skills. In tiny hushed workrooms each stage of the hat is crafted by an all-female team: hand-dyeing, steaming and finishing with the finest ribbons, feathers and flowers that cover every surface. The shop, a stone’s throw from St James’s Palace, has served countless royals (it currently holds a royal warrant from King Charles), along with politicians (Winston Churchill’s order ledger is in the ground-floor heritage room), authors, actors and icons including Jacqueline Kennedy and Princess Diana. The bowler hat was invented here – it was originally commissioned for the gamekeepers of the Holkham estate – and top hats are among the individual orders fulfilled by an expert team on the ground floor. Many creations use vintage materials: “You’re buying into a little piece of history, and it’s so much more special,” says Golding. CC Mary Wing To, whip and harness maker The smoulderingly musky scent of leather is absorbed instantly on a visit to Mary Wing To’s garden workshop in suburban south London. The material is the cornerstone of a luxurious artisanal practice straddling the rare craft of traditional whip and harness making (she was protégé to the Queen’s master saddler) and fashion design and sculpture. Blankets of it are accompanied by a sumptuous marble cutting slab; Tohiti canes for whip shafts; her favourite awls for piercing, scoring and dyeing; mood boards marrying editorials, equestrianism and erotica; and mannequin heads, both equine and human. Wing To discovered leathercraft during her fashion design and technology MA at London College of Fashion, when she undertook a saddlery course at Capel Manor College as its first-ever fashion student, upskilling to produce her equestrian-inspired final collection. That parlayed into an apprenticeship at the Royal Mews, the working stable that oversees royal ceremonial transportation – she was on duty for the wedding of the Prince and Princess of Wales – and proximity to “leathercraft at its highest level”. Whip making came via the tutelage of legend Denis Walmsley. An obsession with discipline – both in the process and finished pieces – has driven her to deliver numerous competition wins for saddlery and wearable arts, and exhibition honours at the V&A. “For me it’s always been about consistency and discipline, and passing on these skills; these incredible legacies.” KB Maya Njie, perfumer The Shoreditch studio of perfumer Maya Njie – a second-storey hideaway bordered by the rumbling beat of the Tube, where she develops genderless and vegan scents and runs private workshops – is a touchingly intimate echo of her home. More vintage boutique than clinician’s lab, it’s a snapshot of her Swedish Gambian heritage and the hub of a nostalgia-riffing creative practice designing biographical fragrances that encapsulate moments, people and places. A mood board-esque wall of thank-you cards, exhibition flyers and her own photographs dominate the entry. Having studied surface design at London’s University of the Arts, she’s still a prolific image maker – each scent comes with an evocative postcard-sized visual and thumbnail colour palette. Paintings are propped against walls, surrounded by an eclectic mix of furniture (“mostly sourced from eBay and antiques markets”) including a German medicine cabinet housing precious olfactory accoutrements such as resins, essential oils, aroma-compounds, cruelty-free musk and molecules, with which she creates her unique blends. The finessed formulas are left to mature then filtered into small batches of scent. Ten years after launching online, she now has eight core perfumes: a personal archive in olfactory form. “There’s an importance in diverse cultural stories being told [via scent], especially when perfumery dates back millennia, long before France was the epicentre of fragrance,” says Njie. “Everyone can take inspiration from a place, but it’s vital to have perfumers telling stories deeply authentic to who they are.” KB Rian Kanduth, gilder Alchemist’s chamber meets forensic laboratory at Rian Kanduth’s diminutive studio in the City & Guilds of London Art School, like a portal to arcane magic. It’s a sensory sweetshop for the investigative decorative arts, where her projects often demand exacting historical knowledge and a scientifically granular handle on environmental factors including heat, light and humidity. Every inch is surrendered to experimentation: cabinets and refrigerators hold pigments and abrasives including rabbit-skin glue, “dragon’s blood” (a crimson tree resin for vibrant glazes) and “dead bugs’ graveyard” (cochineal dye), and test tubes of gold leaf “bling” are tacked to the wall for eye-level inspection. Sensorial instincts are vital because water gilding – the application of a micro-thin layer of metal or other ornamental substrate to a surface – is an art form of more than 18 steps, some going back 5,000 years. Other techniques include pastiglia (intricate paste work patterns), verre églomisé (reverse glass gilding, creating a shimmering effect), sgraffito (scratching a surface layer to reveal a contrasting underlay), gesso and punchwork (stamping patterns into a gilded surface). It “requires us to use all our senses, including smell, to do the right thing”, says Kanduth. “It’s a constant analytical process where we’re perfecting the recipe.” She normally works “upside down and really high” across private homes, artists’ studios, museums and Unesco heritage sites. Like paramedics for at-risk art, she and her team sometimes undertake emergency conservation, from dealing with damaged carvings to time-pressured archaeological digs. KB Kaori Tatebayashi, ceramicist Kaori Tatebayashi’s airy studio is filled with ceramic flowers. There are towering foxgloves suspended along the walls; primroses, miniature iris and hyacinths arranged in a tableau on the floor; and tables topped with fritillaries and full-blown tulips, as well as an unfurling magnolia flower held on a branch. Hand modelling in warm white stoneware, she captures a fleeting moment of the plant’s life, working directly on her kiln shelf. “Once I start I don’t stop – I have to be so quick,” she says of the time constraints of working with clay. Each piece is fired, then left unglazed and undecorated, so that the focus is on the flower’s form. “When the colour is removed, you see plants with a fresh eye.” Born in Arita, Japan, home of Imari porcelain, Tatebayashi studied ceramics at Kyoto City University of Arts before moving to London to attend the Royal College of Art and then relocating permanently in 2001. Alongside her solo exhibitions at Tristan Hoare Gallery, she takes on private commissions and site-specific installations. Her peaceful Deptford studio, hidden at the back of a modern building right on the banks of the Thames (at high tide the water laps just feet from her door), is decorated with antique furniture, cabinets filled with curiosities, books of botanical drawings and a table of plants that she sources from specialist growers, her shared allotment in south London, and sometimes from clients’ gardens. In spring, when her favourite bulbs begin to emerge, her personal life is put on hold. “When they start flowering, I drop everything.” CC Darren Appiagyei, wood sculptor Anchored in the stoic energy of heavy-duty machinery, the workshop of award-winning wood artist Darren Appiagyei in Deptford’s Cockpit Arts studios is a dusty, spit-and-sawdust hub suited to the slow satisfaction of iterative hands-on experimentation. The room he affectionately calls “the shed” is dominated by a hulking lathe, simple workbench and chrome shelving unit brandishing an array of logs. It’s here that self-taught Appiagyei transforms the raw shafts of felled trees – relishing their grains, knots and imperfections – into receptacles at equal turns robust and exquisitely fragile-looking. They’re so finely honed, often featuring wafer-thin walls, that they sometimes resemble ceramics. During a practice he describes as “very meditative, even therapeutic”, he carves into the trunks (all commandeered within a five-mile radius, aligned with his reverence for nature and focus on sustainability), finessing parts of the exterior and leaving others raw to expose the timber’s unique organic patina. Sometimes he uses a pyrography device to scorch tiny dots onto the surface like a 3D pointillist, rendering them “stylistically primitivist but also very refined”. A decade since he graduated in 3D design from Camberwell College of Arts, where he first learnt wood turning, his obsession with the material remains undimmed “because it has a life of its own. It’s wholly its own organism, which keeps it exciting.” KB Carréducker, shoemakers On the wall behind a workbench at Carréducker, the company founded by Deborah Carré and James Ducker in 2004 to make handsewn shoes, is a pegboard featuring the tools of their trade. There are lasting pliers, feathering knives, burnishing irons and the brilliantly named “fudge wheel”, a stitch-marking tool. Nearby there’s a vitrine of maquettes showing different stitch constructions, from blind welt to Norwegian welting. In all, there are 200 steps in making a shoe, says Carré, and how each is executed affects the final balance, proportions and look. They make everything here, from walking boots and derbies to Oxfords and sneakers. Carré describes their house style as “magpie”, which reflects the fact that each design is led by their client’s tastes and preferences. Not a lot has changed in the craft since the Worshipful Company of Cordwainers was granted ordinances in the City of London in 1272; even the business duo’s preferred oak-bark-tanned leather comes from J & FJ Baker in Colyton, Devon, where there has been tanning on site since Roman times. Alongside making bespoke shoes for private clients, the pair also run workshops and courses for amateurs and wannabe shoe-makers in their studio in the Oxo Tower on the Thames. “Our students are attracted by the mindfulness, the focus, the concentration, the mental health benefits of working with their hands,” says Carré. CC Michael Ruh, glass-blower In the southeast London studio of Michael Ruh, the blazing furnace pushes the temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius in summer, and the air is scented with the distinctive perfume of wood smoke and molten beeswax, used to lubricate the glass-blower’s tools. Transforming cullet, a waste product from the optical glass industry, is a visceral and sensory practice, and one where speed and movement is key: malleable molten glass waits for no one. Ruh originally studied fine art before he began working with glass in Belgium. He launched his eponymous studio with partner Natascha Wahl in 2004, and moved to his current mews location in 2013. Alongside his glassware and private commissions, the space hosts occasional workshops in glass engraving, and open studios. It was the constant motion and the possibilities of this challenging material that first captured the imagination of the American-born maker, whose recycled glassware, lighting and tableware are highly sought-after. He blows and shapes sculptural pieces using innovative moulds made in paper or wood, adding organic curves or impressions in the soft glass. His beautiful, functional objects are distinctive for their subtle markings, created with self-made tools. Tumblers are circled with fine lines, often inspired by the light and landscape or the bracing icy winters of his Minnesota childhood; memories that are frozen in time as the glass rapidly cools. CC Tuesday Riddell, lacquerwork artist Odes to the romance, mysteries and beguiling savagery of nature are abundant in Tuesday Riddell’s studio on the banks of south London’s River Wandle. The space hosts micro mises en scènes of shells, leaves and feathers mingling with jars of richly coloured pigments; booklets of gossamer-thin gold and silver leaf; charcoal sketches depicting black cats and earthworms tumbling from seething soil (“five-minute works to get my creative flow moving”); and weathered copies of Angela Carter’s gloriously dark, folklore-twisting novels. Renowned for the endangered, conservation craft of Japanning (lacquerwork), Riddell has always found inspiration in the natural world’s sublimely lethal majesty: “I’m fascinated by the tension between the fragility and the horror of nature. Anything too pleasant feels stale.” This skill, which she learnt during a Painter-Stainers decorative surfaces fellowship at the City & Guilds of London Art School, involves applying 30 to 40 layers of black lacquer – composed of shellac (natural resin) and pigments – to boards, building intense depth. It’s a long process: sanding in between every five or 10 layers, rendering them flush for the next application. Extended drying times mean Riddell often has up to 30 artworks in progress. The final, pictorial element becomes highly nerve-racking – an incorrect stroke can obliterate months of preparation, but the risk, she says, is worth it: “No other process fully captures what I’m imagining. It’s like subconsciously knowing a language you somehow magically speak.” KB Hand & Lock, embroiderers The Fitzrovia HQ of Hand & Lock, Britain’s oldest and most revered embroidery house, is a treasure trove of decorative artistry inconspicuously enclaved behind glazed double doors. Its four storeys have a palpable air of mystique thanks to a stream of confidential projects with its royal, military, fashion couture and pop culture clientele. There’s a jewel box shop whose wooden drawers cradle glittering gemlike brooches, insignia, cords and coloured fringes; a school; traditional and digital ateliers; and a samples-packed bead room. Key techniques include goldwork, using metal threads and bullion to add volume and texture; couture-associated tambour beading, which has a flawlessly uniform fluidity; and silk shading, where threads coalesce into a painterly breed of realism often used to depict flowers or animals. Work they can divulge: items for King Charles III’s coronation, including ceremonial and regimental garments, plus former House of Commons leader Penny Mordaunt’s cape dress and headband; the winged jacket for Elton John’s Who Believes in Angels? album cover; and work for Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein and Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights. According to Sophie Carr, who ran emerging talent incubator The Hand & Lock Prize for Embroidery for eight years after winning it in 2011, they recently embroidered a luxury train carriage’s interior. Hand & Lock also creates two main annual collections, sells YouTube-tutorial-accompanied taster kits, and hosts courses with The National Gallery, V&A and Kew Gardens. Why the booming popularity? “Detail, a satisfyingly slow process and desire for modern heirlooms,” says Carr. KB Bellerby & Co, globemakers The cavernous, corrugated-roof workshop of Bellerby & Co Globemakers in Stoke Newington feels more like a film set than a 21st-century studio. It’s a vivid tableau of the myriad skills that go into making each bespoke globe: sets of gores hang from pegs and string across windows (each globe has 12 or 24 of these panels that are dampened and then precisely applied to the surface of the sphere), and shelves are topped with globes in all sizes awaiting the meticulous hand painting and illustration that is applied by a team of watercolour artists. When Peter Bellerby was searching for a globe for his father almost two decades ago, he couldn’t find anything that fitted the bill. So he went on a two-year odyssey to create one, and launched his eponymous firm in the process. “Globes are a wonderful convergence of the arts and the sciences,” he says of the skills in engineering, geography and artistry required. Each globe takes weeks or even months to make, and is a work of art, customised with family histories, past travels, migration routes and themes. The slow and meticulous process of making by hand is celebrated: apprentices here train for at least a year before producing the 22cm desk globe. The biggest – a show-stopping 152cm diameter model created for the new National Geographic museum in Washington, DC – is the largest hand-painted globe in the world, and smoothly spins on an axis. CC Kyriacos Hadjikyriacou, pleater Secluded in a vast hangar on a Tottenham industrial estate, Kyriacos Hadjikyriacou, the UK’s most revered pleater, is working among a shadowy horde of industrial machinery (“some can create 1,500 styles, others just one”), a towering backdrop of fabric bolts, and two gleaming steel steam boxes that hold court like bonfire-powered beach huts. There are also reams of delicate textiles, artfully gathered, ruched, scored and creased (designs can be machine-birthed and hand-finished, and vice versa). The dichotomy of his work – clients include students, hair academies and high-profile fashion houses such as Alexander McQueen and Victoria Beckham – demands both technical acumen (his career began in hydroponics and agricultural engineering) and a craftsman’s dexterity. “Pleating is geometry. If you don’t know geometry, you’re a folder, not a pleater,” says Hadjikyriacou. Original inventions are key to his success (he’s now in his late 70s), alongside precision replicas. One of his favourite concoctions is a white satin crown-pleated coffin inlay, “a design so unusual it took a year to develop”. Inspiration lies everywhere: honeycombs, mushroom innards, hieroglyphics, “If you can think it, you can do it.” KB Manuel Mazzotti, bookbinder Located in an unassuming east London residential complex, the studio of award-winning bookbinder Manuel Mazzotti is a hive of carefully controlled creative chaos. He is a virtuoso in finding new ways to bind, cover and encase printed material (books, but often in unconventional form), and signs of an impatient mind relentlessly in prototyping mode abound: a sprawling plan chest strewn with mid-assemblage projects; plotters (for precision cutting); bone folders (for creasing); and Japanese stepped rulers beloved by Mazzotti for “their simple effective clarity”. Images from favourite works crowd the walls and a circa-1910 heat press (refurbished to run on electricity) sits majestically in the corner while a pair of Japanese Daruma dolls – talismans of goal setting – keep watch. Both aesthetician and technician, Italian-born Mazzotti studied mechanical engineering then transportation design before going to Switzerland’s prestigious Centro del Bel Libro to learn bookbinding. He famously uses challenging materials (recently, Carrara marble) and wildly proportioned designs – such as the supersized “clamshell” format for artist Hormazd Narielwalla’s Sky in a Box – in his creations. His personal work teases the dichotomy of raw, salvaged materials with pristine detailing, emphasising physical nuance. An avid book collector who scours bookshops for special editions like others hunt rare vinyl, Mazzotti is emphatic about their emotional magnetism, noting a rising appetite from creative agencies, artists and families reimagining heirlooms. “Books are powerful objects. They’ve always represented knowledge and status, but now, as we question what will remain of our digital footprint in 100 years, they also mean continuity.” KB Blenheim Forge, knife makers Aptly for a brand birthed in 2014 as a DIY endeavour in a south London back garden – “We somehow forged a knife in conditions where it shouldn’t have succeeded, then spent years obsessively trying to replicate it,” says Jon Warshawsky, one of the three founders – entering the railway arch home of small-batch knife makers Blenheim Forge is like slipping into a bricolage steampunk dreamscape. After passing through iron gates wrought into organic patterns and a small courtyard amassed with metal ephemera, I clamber through a wooden door-within-a-door camouflaged by a floor-to-ceiling mural of a bull and a jester. Inside, the aroma of maple wood erupts as a knife’s handle is put through its bandsaw paces. The knives are created by fusing multiple bars of steel, a sandwich that’s battered into shape via power hammers or anvil-based hand-forging. They’re then heat-treated and tempered for durability and sharpness, ground down, polished, etched and sharpened. The workshop, separated from the display-based front area by a Crittall glass partition, is packed with machinery for specific procedures to hone high-performance knives for professional chefs and dedicated home cooks. Heavily inspired by Japanese knives, with names including Gyuto, Nakiri and Santoku, each is forged from a combination of steels to be precise, strong and balanced, but adapted for everyday multipurpose Western culinary sensibilities, including being lighter and more comfortable to handle. Constantly innovating, Warshawsky and his co-founders, James Ross-Harris and Richard Warner, flex their creative muscles on a bimonthly special, using new techniques or developing genres such as an oyster shucker or barbecue knife. They recently commissioned their own steel, which will, says Warshawsky, “level up everything we make”. KB Clio Peppiatt, fashion designer Clio Peppiatt’s inaugural Knightsbridge flagship is a boudoir of a boutique birthed with modern showgirls in mind. Seashell cocktail goblets, sumptuous carpets and soft fabric wall drapes in dreamy baby blue evoke silver screen-era Vegas and create a cinematic backdrop for contour-caressing bridal and evening wear embellished head to hem in traditional Tambour beading and hand-embroidery. Modern heirlooms are devoted to the joy of dressing up – “I see my pieces as wearable art that celebrates the wearer,” says Peppiatt. Minidresses contain approximately 250,000 recycled glass beads; long dresses half a million. It’s all steeped in a familial legacy of female entrepreneurialism stretching back eight generations. Peppiatt’s great-grandmother, the first in the lineage to professionalise crafting, was a lacemaker specialising in women’s gloves, and Peppiatt’s grandmother taught her artisanal embroidery skills. Peppiatt hand-draws and paints every design – often playful motifs such as coral reefs and cactus-bearing desertscapes – in her west London studio, and collaborates with a Mumbai-based atelier on everything from prototypes to final pieces, “because their skills are like nothing else”. Those designs become marks on tracing paper via a “tattoo-gun-style holepunch”, are stretched across a table-sized embroidery loom, then worked on from underneath using a hooked needle. “It’s very intuitive,” she explains, “because you can’t see your hands while working.” Has her label’s sensibility changed since its 2015 inception? “It still has a maximalist spirit, but with joy and a sense of femininity that is felt not performed.” KB

item.title: UK flight delays after NATS technical failure hits Heathrow, Gatwick and other airports
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.22
Several major UK airports have experienced delays due to an air traffic control technical failure. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has identified the issue, but there is no certainty in whether air traffic will go back to normal today. The national air traffic control service (NATS) warned in their latest statement on X: “We have identified that the issue was in our flight processing system. Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible. We recognise the ongoing disruption to travel, for which we sincerely apologise.” The statement continued: “Flights are still departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time. We will provide further updates as soon as possible.” Heathrow Airport shared an update on its X account: “The air traffic control service is experiencing a technical issue which is impacting departing flights at UK airports. Arriving flights are not currently impacted. We are supporting our local NATS team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.” However, some passengers arriving at Heathrow reported knock-on disruption, including being kept on aircraft after landing. Other airports such as Birmingham Airport and Jersey Airport have also issued statements, but neither NATS nor the airports have given a firm timeline for a return to normal operations. According to the Financial Times, Eurocontrol – the organisation responsible for coordinating air traffic across Europe – warned that disruption to airspace over London, southern England and Wales could continue until 9pm on Tuesday. Passengers should check the status of their flight directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruption include: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport

item.title: Paris could soon be just a train ride away for East London
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.62
Stratford International could become a new hub for European rail travel, as Virgin Trains considers stopping in East London when it launches its new cross-Channel services to rival Eurostar. According to the rail regulator, the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), Virgin will be allowed to operate up to 20 daily return services between London and Paris, Brussels or Amsterdam from October 2030, potentially ending Eurostar's monopoly since 1994. The proposed timetable for Paris initially sees six return services per day, increasing to 10 from April 2031 and 13 from October 2031. Following the ORR's decision, there are talks of Virgin’s new international services stopping at Stratford International as well as the usual Eurostar stop at St Pancras International. Sir Stephen Timms, MP for East Ham, has welcomed the possibility of international trains stopping in East London, as it would promote regeneration in the area. Virgin Trains has plans to invest £700m in the project and create hundreds of jobs in the UK, including skilled jobs at the Temple Mills depot in East London. The MP has previously called for more rail services to stop at Stratford International. Responding to his calls for Virgin to consider a stop in East London, a spokeswoman for Virgin Trains said: “We have recently been awarded track access on London St Pancras Highspeed and will be bringing investment and new skilled jobs to the Temple Mills depot in East London.” She added: “Virgin is looking forward to exploring additional stops, including Stratford International.” Virgin is not quite ready to hit the rails yet, as the company still has to secure access to rail tracks through the Channel Tunnel (owned by Eurotunnel) and European rail networks, as well as obtain the necessary safety approvals. If everything goes to plan, Virgin intends to launch services from London to Paris in October 2030, with Brussels and Amsterdam also forming part of its planned European network.

item.title: 9 best hotels in Jaipur, India's beautiful Pink City
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.62
As one of the most beautiful corners in India, it's only fitting that the best hotels in Jaipur are among some of the prettiest in the world. With its scope of stunning palaces, formidable forts, and vibrant markets, Jaipur reveals itself to tourists like no other city, and checking in to one of these tried and tested Condé Nast Traveller-approved hotels guarantees a bucket-list stay fulfilled.
