From palace hotels that offer the royal treatment to bijou retreats full of colour and character, here we list some of our favourite places to stay in the Rajasthan capital. Editor's picks of the best hotels in and near Jaipur - For honeymoons: Samode Palace - For families: The Oberoi Rajvilas - For a boutique stay: Villa Palladio Jaipur What is the best time to visit Jaipur? The best time to visit Goa is from November to February. The heat and humidity give way to more pleasant sunny days by December, and the waves are gentler during this time. December also brings the Christmas spirit to several local homes, and bakeries and decades-old stores stock up on local Christmas sweets like kalkal, dodol and neureos. This is also peak tourist season in Goa, which means hotel and flight prices shoot up at this time. When is the off season in Jaipur? The off-season in Jaipur, from April to October, brings sweltering summer temperatures followed by rains. This period is characterised by lower accommodation rates and fewer tourists, making it a cost-effective time to visit. The heat and humidity can make outdoor activities less enjoyable, but the quieter streets and discounted stays offer a more relaxed travel experience. How many days are enough for a trip to Jaipur? A three to four-day trip to Jaipur is ideal for uncovering the city's rich heritage and culture. Start by exploring the grand Amer Fort and its stunning views of the city. Visit the City Palace to admire its opulent architecture and museum exhibits. Jaipur is also famous for its bustling markets, so a trip to Nehru Bazaar is a must if you are in search of traditional juttis, while Tripolia Bazaar is renowned for its beautiful bangles. How we choose the best hotels in Jaipur Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels. More India recommendations This article was originally published on Cntraveller.in

item.title: 14 best hotel resorts in Mallorca to book for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.48
Mallorca does resorts with more subtlety than most islands its size. The infrastructure is there, of course: beach clubs, sprawling spas, kids’ clubs, adults-only sanctuaries, golf courses curling through the hills. But the best resort stays here do not feel air-dropped in. They tend to grow out of the landscape or the island’s own visual language, whether that means a honey-stone hill village above the northeast coast, a 14th-century finca estate folded into vineyards, or a cliff-hugging hideaway where the Tramuntana mountains drop theatrically into the sea. Even the bigger, shinier properties still feel distinctly Mallorcan rather than generically Mediterranean. The island also makes resort-hopping by mood unusually easy. In the north and northeast, around Formentor, Alcúdia and Playa de Muro, the draw is beach life, family ease and a kind of clean, athletic outdoorsiness shaped by cycling routes, sailing and long pale bays. The southeast, around Porto Petro, softens into quieter coves and low-key fishing villages. Inland and toward the west, the tempo shifts again. Here, resorts become more introspective: monastery estates, adults-only retreats among pine trees, well-being hideaways where the point is not to be entertained but restored. item.title: The Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is autumn's hottest culture ticket – here's how to get tickets to the sold-out exhibition
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.46
When news emerged in 2025 that the Bayeux Tapestry would be returning to the UK following a historic loan agreement with France, it sparked a waiting list to rival a Harry Styles concert. Once the first batch of tickets was finally released in July, they sold out in record time – driving the highest single-day of ticket sales in the British Museum’s history. Over 80,000 people joined the online queues trying to secure the first batch of tickets, which sold out in just 24 hours, generating more than £2.4 million in ticket sales. Further fanning the flames of excitement was the tapestry's secret arrival in London, under police escort and before a select crowd of insiders at 2:50am. Such anticipation around a museum exhibit is largely unheard of, making this a particularly landmark coup for the British Museum. The agreement marks the tapestry's first return to England since its creation nearly 1000 years ago, leaving history buffs itching to see it on home soil. Instagram content British Museum director Nick Cullinan told BBC News following its arrival: "We've just witnessed something rather extraordinary, which is the arrival of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum – but specifically it is returning to England for the first time in almost 1,000 years. Depicting the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings, the Bayeux Tapestry is widely regarded as the only surviving pictorial account of the 1066 Norman Conquest, marking the last time England was successfully invaded and the year from which the modern monarchy dates itself. Ahead of the exhibition, the British Museum had stated: “One of the wonders of the medieval world, the Tapestry offers a vision of life in 11th-century England both before and after the Conquest, from castles, warfare and ships to clothing, food and furniture. Likely commissioned by a Norman patron and made by English embroiderers, using manuscript drawings from Canterbury, the Tapestry is both a precious historical record and a remarkable work of art.” A glimpse into the exhibition Earlier this month, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were joined by French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte for a preview of the exhibition. The King gave a speech highlighting the significance of the loan – first requested in the 1930s and finally secured nearly a century later – and took the opportunity to celebrate the friendship between the two countries. "The tapestry's story is one of ambition and uncertainty, of oaths and journeys, of ships, councils, kings, comets and consequences, yet it is not merely an English story, nor only a Norman one. Indeed, from the moment of its creation, it may have brought together our two peoples," said the King. "I cannot help but feel that its protagonists, on both sides of the Channel, would look with satisfaction on the Franco-British gathering here today, and be pleased that our two great nations, which share such fundamental values, have prospered together – across the tides of history," he continued. Curators at the British Museum have decided to exhibit the tapestry flat. Visitors entering the darkened gallery will see the tapestry displayed in a long, illuminated glass cabinet, allowing them to move alongside it as the story of the events leading up to the Norman Conquest unfolds. To give more people across the country the opportunity to enjoy this unique piece of history, the British Museum has launched the Bayeux Around Britain programme. As well as online events – including a lecture on 25 September with exhibition curator Professor Michael Lewis and medievalist Professor Leonie Hicks – more than 60 museums and heritage sites will host a series of activities inspired by the exhibition. To learn more about the activities, visit the dedicated page here. How to get tickets to see the Bayeux Tapestry The 70-metre-long tapestry will be on view at the museum from September 2026 to July 2027 – and while the first batch of tickets (spanning 10 September to 31 December 2026) has sold out, tickets for 1 January–31 March 2027 will be available to purchase on 21 October 2026, with British Museum members getting priority booking from 6 October. Tickets for April–11 July will be released in early 2027. There are no walk-in tickets, so advance booking is essential to see this historic exhibition. According to the British Museum, the next block of bookings will open up later in the year. You can sign up for the venue's newsletter to get specific release dates – since tickets sold out within 24 hours last time, demand is expected to be very high. Find out more about the exhibition via the British Museum here.

item.title: This medieval Spanish city is Europe's best-kept secret for active travellers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.93
In case you haven’t noticed, running, cycling and endurance sports are booming. People are signing up for marathons, Ironman triathlons and ultra-marathons in their droves. This surge has had a huge effect on travel patterns – now, more than ever, athletes are travelling to international races and seamlessly weaving training into their holiday plans. As a member of the Irish triathlon team, and a three-time Ironman finisher, I'm one of these people. In my endeavours to bring together my love of sport and travel, I've planned trips that explore a destination's active side, while still ticking classic travel boxes. In doing so, I've realised how valuable a handy guide is when planning these types of trips. Our collective love affair with suffering to get a finisher’s medal has never been stronger. As a result, classic cycling and running destinations such as Mallorca get three-deep with pelotons come April, Tenerife's Teide Loop now needs booking and Font-Romeu regulars are grumbling about rising costs. This July, I travelled from London to compete for my country at the World Triathlon European Middle Distance Triathlon Championships in Banyoles. It's a small city, 20 minutes up the road from Girona. The race course was epic and intimidating: swim 1.9km in the stunningly blue L’Estany Banyoles lake, ride 85km along the smooth-as-butter roads between Banyoles and Girona with some hills thrown in and run 14km by the lake to cheering crowds. The run was supposed to be a half Marathon, but due to the intense heatwave sweeping across Europe, the officials shortened the course by 7km for safety. For the duration of race week, I stayed in the heart of Girona and quickly discovered it truly is the European capital for travellers seeking an active holiday. Girona has that magical and rare combination of everything an active traveller seeks. The roads are almost free of potholes, and drivers here understand how to respect cyclists and runners. There are varied routes ranging from flat and fast to punchy hills for a challenge, with epic views to boot. And, finally, there are plenty of shops and services within the city’s picturesque walls to cater to any athlete's needs. Hundreds of pro cyclists, runners and triathletes live in Girona not for the scenery alone but because the roads are quieter, the tarmac is fresh, and you can climb Rocacorba or freewheel the Costa Brava within 20 minutes of your front door. Georgia Taylor Brown, a multiple world champion in triathlon and Gold, Silver and Bronze medalist across the 2020 and 2024 Olympics for Team GB in triathlon, sums up why she loves living in Girona: “When I first visited Girona, I instantly fell in love," she says. "Training is simple and peaceful here. There are so many options for road cycling on super-quiet roads or beautiful gravel loops that go on forever. Also so many running options; if you want trails, hills, flat, track, Girona has it all. There’s also now a super cool performance lab (H Lab) for those wanting to gain the extra few per cent.” What keeps pulling me back to this city isn't only the terrain, it's that Girona makes living an active lifestyle very easy. Mornings start with proper coffee, often roasted by fellow athletes, in the shadow of Girona’s Gothic cathedral, to the soundtrack of whirring freehubs of the cyclists rolling past on their carbon-framed bikes. Evenings end in one of the many bars and restaurants lining the old town’s cobbled streets (think Barcelona’s Las Ramblas, but far more relaxed). If you’re looking for a rest day activity, head to the cathedral steps (Game of Thrones fans will recognise them instantly), the Jewish Quarter's tangled lanes, and a walk along the medieval city walls for views over the rooftops to the Pyrenees. Girona is a city where I can train like an athlete and seamlessly transition into holiday mode as soon as a session ends. Here is my ultimate guide to tackling this medieval Spanish city like a pro. The ultimate Girona guide for active travellers The best active routes in Girona Cycling Rocacorba, with 12km at 6.5 per cent, is the climb everyone talks about – and for good reason. The opening half lets you settle in, but don’t get lulled into a false sense of security. Ride it early if you can; it gets hot and exposed later in the day. Els Àngels is the more forgiving classic and a much more social climb. It’s shorter, gentler and more rhythmical, which is why locals use it for everything from recovery spins to threshold work. The road is shaded in parts, the gradients are steadier, and the monastery at the top gives it a proper destination feel. The Empordà loop is where the roads flatten out into long, quiet lanes through villages, farmland and open stretches. It’s ideal for steady endurance riding, especially if you want to add volume without constantly thinking about traffic or junctions. Check the forecast, and if you’re heading toward the coast, expect the return leg to feel very different depending on the wind. Running The Carrilet greenway follows an old railway line out of the city, traffic-free and shaded, while the river paths along the Onyar and Ter make for an easy recovery loop. Swimming Head to Lake Banyoles (L'Estany Banyoles), Europe's finest swimming lake, and the swim venue for this year's European championship. If you prefer a sea swim, go to the coves around Aiguablava on the Costa Brava. The best restaurants in Girona La Comuna For the most important meal of the day, La Comuna is where to head, tucked away from the town centre its the perfect place to spot some of the pro athletes that call Girona home. The team are welcoming and the coffee is incredible. Website: lacomuna.co Brovola When I need quick carbs straight after a ride, Brovola’s handmade Focaccia sandwiches are my go-to. Most of their sandwiches are savoury and full of local ingredients and organic meat, but they even have a Nutella-laden version if you need to get those calories into you ASAP. Website: bravola-focacceria.com Idle Hands The ultimate brunch/ lunch spot in Girona. They are also open on Thursday and Friday nights for a well-earned burger made with grass-fed beef. The garlic miso burger is my favourite. They also offer GF versions of their burgers, as well as veggie and pescatarian options. Website: idlehandsgirona.com The best cafés in Girona Oniria A staple of the city's cafe culture and well worth the visit. They also offer Barista and coffee art courses with the café’s Founder Jannik. You can bring back more than extra fitness from your holiday in Girona; perfecting your latte art is a worthy skill to learn during your rest time. Website: oniriacafe.com Classic Coffee Bar Opened in June 2026 as the first café in Spain pouring Illest Drinks, this is the kind of spot where a flat white turns into a conversation served by baristas who are passionate about cycling and triathlon as much as coffee. Classic also stocks some top-notch gear from Surpas if you’re looking to buy new jerseys and bibs. Website: instagram.com Maison Marcel If there’s one thing cyclists, runners and triathletes can all agree on, it's that a pastry is a non-negotiable after a long session. Refuelling with pastries from Maison Marcel is a pilgrimage for anyone training in Girona. Their Jamon Iberico brioche roll is so simple but so tasty. Website: maisonmarcel.eu Where to go shopping in Girona Velodrome Set in a former classic cinema, this is definitely the world’s most beautiful cycling shop, and that’s before you even consider their bike stock. Though, you're missing a trick if you don't also seek out the smaller independent shops sprinkled around the city. Website: velodrom.cc Tata Bikes A family-run cycling boutique in the old Jewish Quarter. After my handlebars got mangled in transit to Girona, Stelian, the owner, immediately stopped what he was doing and sorted them within 15 minutes. I cannot recommend a visit enough for repairs, rentals and beautifully curated gear from a husband-and-wife team who treat every customer like a regular. Website: tatabikes.com Temple Running Stocks road and trail shoes and apparel from Norda, On, Satisfy and more, alongside organising regular runs and events to support the running community. The owner, Aleix, is a talented ultra runner and knows what he's talking about. I picked up a pair of their socks for my race, and they are now my go-to race sock. Website: temple-running.com Where to stay in Girona Hotel Nord 1901 Based in the old town, this little hotel has thought of everything for travellers with bikes. There’s secure bike storage, a pool for recovery and the team have great connections with mechanics throughout the city. The hotel has eighteen rooms that fill quickly with kit bags all season, so book well in advance. Website: nord1901.com Gran Ultònia Offers a secluded rooftop bar if you want to unwind after a day on the trails. This is the perfect place to stay if you’re travelling with a group, as they offer group cycling info sessions on where to cycle, as well as that important secure bike storage. Website: hotelsultoniagirona.com Off Grid Girona Further out of the city, in La Garrotxa, a rustic-luxury 17th-century masia built around cycling, yoga and communal, locally-sourced dining. Off Grid is really the perfect place to unwind after a day on the trails. If travelling in a group, the entire property can be booked. Also, Off Grid isn’t a cyclist-only destination; they host yoga retreats and easy hiking excursions for those who may want to holiday at a slower pace. Website: offgridgirona.com

It may not have the private island feel of the Maldives or the Indiana Jones giant fauna and tropical jungle of the Seychelles, but a Mauritius escape offers faultless service, white sand beaches, activities (golf, and then some more golf, hiking and paddle boarding) and farm-to-table gastronomy. With its burgeoning boutique rum industry and host of emerging artisans – from textiles to ceramics – be sure to pack an empty suitcase for your return journey. The Mauritius resorts in our edit feature some of the world's top luxury chains as well as some exceptional homegrown brands who are shaping the country’s industry with a proud, hands-on approach. Much of the best hotels in Mauritius are spread out around the coastline, from One&Only Le Saint Géran in Poste de Flacq on the north eastern side of the island to Heritage Le Telfair in Bel Ombre on the south west coast. If you're excited to snorkel in Mauritius, you'll find the best conditions along the west side of the island, particularly near Flic En Flac beach. For easy swimming, opt for a hotel on the west coast where the seas tend to be calmer and warmer. For complete privacy, Shangri-La Le Touessrok is located on its own private island. What is the best time of year to visit Mauritius? June marks the beginning of the Mauritian dry season, and while it's not the hottest time of year to visit the island, temperatures sit comfortably between 20 and about 28 degrees celsius. It's officially ‘winter’ there at this time, and the season lasts until September. The hottest time of year to visit is typically between December and January, but there is also a higher chance of rainfall and the weather feels humid.
