item.title: The High-Altitude Journey of the World’s Most Famous Adventure Cat
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.31
Simon the adventure cat (Photo: Courtesy of JJ Yosh) Had JJ Yosh, an adventure content creator based in Boulder, Colorado, simply taken his cat, Simon, on a handful of hikes and posted the videos online, I would have dismissed it as a pet-thetic social media stunt. But a decade after adopting the black Bombay cat, the duo—better known to millions as Backpacking Kitty on Instagram and TikTok—has built something far more remarkable. Together they’ve hiked the Austrian Alps, whitewater rafted California’s Sacramento River, climbed a volcano in Guatemala, and traveled to more than 15 countries and four continents. They’ve flown on over 100 flights, including on a seaplane, and kayaked some of the most remote waterways in the world, taking an audience of 11 million followers along with them, and making Simon less of a novelty and more like a bona fide field companion. Now Yosh has something even more ambitious in mind. He’s preparing to take Simon on a multi-year Seven Summits spree. “I’m positive he’s the only cat who has summited a dozen of Colorado’s 14ers,” Yosh says of Simon who he rescued from euthanasia in 2016. Yet even those accomplishments, and, arguably, the title of one of the most famous cats in the world, pale beside this latest odyssey. Over the next three years, they plan to tackle the tallest mountain on every continent: Denali, Mount Kilimanjaro, Aconcagua, Mount Elbrus, Vinson Massif, Puncak Jaya, and the world’s highest peak, Mount Everest. Before you picture a cat being hauled into Everest’s notorious Death Zone—a place so hostile to life it contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level—rest easy. “I’m definitely not taking Simon to the summit. I’m not risking his life,” Yosh says. While Yosh makes his push for the top, Simon will be living the considerably cushier life at Everest Base Camp with a dedicated pet sitter, people he already knows and trusts. Yosh is emphatic that Simon’s health and safety come first. “How high he goes depends entirely on the mountain,” Yosh says. That means, for Everest, Base Camp is his ceiling. “Nothing above it, no exceptions.” For Kilimanjaro and Aconcagua? Those are non-technical walk-ups, so there is more room. “He could go higher than base camp on those, and how much higher gets decided on the ground rather than promised in advance.” As for everywhere else, Yosh will assess each peak one at a time, and veterinary opinions will inform each decision. Yosh says, “ If the answer is that it is too high for a cat, that is the end of it. He does not go.” It’s all part of the careful balance Yosh has spent the past decade striking with his feline partner. Simon may be born for adventure—while he does trek via leash, he’s happiest riding Yosh’s shoulders through forests and across alpine trails, even snowboarding—he’s still a cat, with very real limitations. For example, while Yosh was on a Mount Baker crevasse rescue training ahead of his Seven Summits bid recently, Simon wasn’t practicing self-arrests. Which begs the question: How do you prepare a house cat for extreme altitude? After all, Everest Base Camp sits at a breath-stealing 17,598 feet. The answer starts at home. In Boulder, where the pair live at roughly 6,000 feet above sea level, acclimatization is woven into everyday life. Yosh’s home—playfully known as “the house his cat built”—is tucked into a rocky cliff and outfitted with an indoor climbing wall scaled by both owner and pet. Outside, Colorado’s high country is Simon’s natural conditioning ground, where regular mountaineering outings have gradually exposed him to thinner air—one might say the purrfect conditions—long before the Himalayas come into view. Yosh has even taken Simon on technical rope climbs, securing him a small-dog harness. And when it comes to gear, Simon is just as outfitted as his owner: Yosh has assembled a wardrobe for Simon to rival any serious adventurer’s, with specialized gear for seemingly every climate, condition, and expedition. Add to that the deep relationship these two have built. Even talking about the possibility of something happening to Simon makes Yosh visibly shaken. The depth of that bond was forged early. Not long after Yosh adopted Simon, he left the cat with a friend while filming a commercial in Bolivia. What Yosh didn’t learn until later was that Simon had gone missing for three days. “Thankfully, they didn’t tell me at the time,” Yosh says. “They’d put up missing posters everywhere, but I had no idea.” Even now, the memory rattles him. “If that happened today and I found out while I was on a mountain, I’d turn around. I wouldn’t be able to finish the climb,” he says. “You have to be in a good mental place to climb a mountain, and I wouldn’t be.” “This work can be so taxing and draining. You question why you’re doing it over and over again,” Yosh says. “That’s where having Simon is such a huge emotional pillow. The hardest moments usually aren’t the scary, high-adrenaline ones. They’re when the weight of the whole expedition catches up with you.” Whether he’s just finished an ultrarun or a grueling climb, Yosh knows there’s one constant: Simon, curled up in the tent ready for a cuddle at the end of the day. In a life all about relentless forward motion, that ritual has become the reset that keeps him going. It will be tested during their next challenge. But first, there are the logistics to work through. Namely, the travel concerns of hop-scotching the planet with a cat. Fortunately, this isn’t Simon’s first rodeo. He has a U.S. ID card and an E.U. pet passport that allows him to easily cross borders, and he doesn’t fly cargo. “But of course he has to get all of these health certificates for each country,” Yosh says. Then there’s the tricky reality of lengthy flights and layovers. Naturally, I had to ask, does Simon get jet lag? “Simon gets so excited every time we reach a new hotel or destination,” Yosh says. “He’s like ready to go.” Apparently, when you’re an international adventuring cat of mystery, the only thing tougher than Everest is waiting for room service. That, and then clawing your way into mountaineering history.

item.title: Colorado’s Maroon Bells Are Closed After a Second Climber Has Died in Less Than a Week
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.30
Responders with Mountain Aspen Rescue evacuated a deceased climber on September 6 using a technical lowering system (Photo: Photo courtesy of MRA) The U.S. Forest Service temporarily closed all climbing access to Colorado’s Maroon Peak on September 8, 2026, to recover the body of a climber who had fallen off the mountain. The death marked the first of two fatal mountaineering accidents on Colorado’s famed 14er summits in less than a week. Officials have not released the names, sex, or ages of either person. On September 8, authorities embarked on a recovery mission for the body of a climber who went missing six days earlier, on September 2, according to the responding agency, Mountain Rescue Aspen (MRA). To aid the recovery, the U.S. Forest Service closed climbing access to Maroon Peak, including the standard route from West Maroon Creek and the traverse from North Maroon Peak. After the climber was reported missing on September 2, rescuers found notes in their vehicle parked at the trailhead. Based on these notes, responders conducted aerial searches in the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness, a remote alpine area that contains six peaks over 14,000 feet, including the iconic maroon-colored twin peaks known as the Maroon Bells and Snowmass Mountain. “During the aerial search, the climber was located deceased and tentatively identified in very technical and difficult terrain to access,” MRA wrote in a statement. In an unrelated incident on September 6, a second climber died after falling from the north face of Castle Peak, located about 12 miles south of Aspen. An all-volunteer team of 21 members responded on the ground and by helicopter. Rebecca Rees, a dental anesthesiologist, witnessed the September 6 fall while hiking with a group between Castle and Conundrum Peaks. Rees, 44, lives in a suburb of Denver and has been climbing Colorado 14ers since 2017. She said she had been on this specific climb around five times. “There had been a rockfall all day from Conundrum going into the lake, so we were used to hearing these rocks fall into the lake,” she said. “At 12:25 P.M., we heard the rocks again but it was a different sound. I looked over and I saw this gentleman tumbling down the mountain. It was horrifying because it was not a fall that would be survivable.” Rees estimated that the man initially fell about 30 feet, and then continued to tumble hundreds more down the mountain. It’s not clear how or why he fell, she said. Her group called emergency services, and yelled at the man, but he was unresponsive. Looking up-slope, she said they saw his sunglasses and water bottles in a debris field. “Mountain Rescue Aspen personnel reached the climber at approximately 3:58 P.M. and determined the individual had sustained injuries that were not survivable,” MRA wrote. “Team members then carefully evacuated the climber from the mountain using a technical lowering system.” Located in Colorado’s Elk Range, the Maroon Bells are one of the most photographed destinations in the state, and encompass Maroon Peak and North Maroon Peak. The peaks have earned their nickname “Deadly Bells“—the mountains are highly technical, dangerous, and extremely difficult, according to the nonprofit that does service work on the state’s highest peaks, Colorado Fourteeners Initiative. “These mountains are known for having a lot of loose rock and being fairly dangerous,” Rees told Outside. “Up close, the rock is very loose and unforgiving. Route-finding is difficult, and it’s very easy to take a wrong step or have the wrong handhold and fall,” she said. Incredibly steep terrain also means seemingly innocuous mishaps can quickly become deadly. In May, a hiker slid 200 feet down the Maroon Bells after slipping at an elevation of around 11,300 feet. In August, Colorado hiker Brandon Hinkle was completing the Maroon Bells Traverse when he tumbled 500 feet down a sheer rock face and suffered multiple serious injuries. Rees reiterated the importance of traveling with a buddy, especially in dangerous terrain. “Without even realizing it in the moment, you’re constantly checking in with each other when you’re hiking up,” she said. “Having that constant feedback and another opinion is helpful checks and balances.” And if you’re not feeling it, Rees said known when to turn around can save lives. “The mountain will be there forever, and it’s okay to get to a certain point and realize today is not the day,” she said. MRA also reminds backcountry travelers to leave a detailed itinerary with a trusted person before departing, including the intended route, expected return time, and contingency plans. Anyone traveling in the backcountry should also carry appropriate equipment, be prepared for rapidly changing mountain conditions, and always bring a reliable two-way satellite communication device when traveling in areas without cell service. “We’re not going to stop hiking these peaks,” Rees added. “It’s traumatizing but, just be safe and be prepared. Know when to stop, and know your limits.”

item.title: 2 Men Tried to Bail in Wyoming’s Cirque of the Towers. They Ended Up Staying the Night on Pingora Peak.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.03
With only a few hours to spare before sunset, the rescue had to wait until the next morning to head in (Photo: Courtesy of Tip Top Search and Rescue) Two stranded climbers had to spend the night on Pingora Peak, a nearly 12,000-foot granite mountain in the Wind River Range of Wyoming, before being rescued by lifesaving crews. On August 20, the duo tried to bail on a climbing route when their rope got stuck while rappelling, leaving them unable to descend. It was around 5 P.M. when they hit their SOS button from a ledge, according to responding agency Tip Top Search and Rescue. With only a few hours to spare before sunset, the rescue had to wait until the next morning. Around 7 A.M., a search-and-rescue group set in to rescue the two climbers. Two Lander Search and Rescue (LSAR) high-angle rescue teams, a specialized emergency response unit trained to reach and recover people from steep faces, also took part. “Multiple attempts were made to deliver long-line supplies to the two stranded climbers, but due to the wind and the clearance of the rotor blades, it was aborted,” Tip Top SAR said in a statement. “The two LSAR climbers were deployed. Once LSAR reached the two climbers, they lowered both to the base of Pingora.” One of the climbers was wearing a bright orange jacket, which helped the team spot the duo on their first pass into the Cirque, Tip Top wrote. “Despite spending a chilly night on the side of Pingora, the rescued climbers reported that they were okay, just thirsty and tired,” responders wrote. “Both were uninjured and declined transport. The rescued climbers continued their trip and hiked out.” Pingora Peak is a famed summit that forms the Cirque of the Towers, a granite amphitheater of jagged peaks in the southern part of the Winds. It’s unclear what route the two were on, but Pingora Peak is considered to be a “low-hanging fruit of accessible alpine climbing in the Wind River Range,” Colorado climber Adam McClatchie told Outside. Pingora Peak is included in the 50 Classic Climbs of North America, a list of coveted climbs made famous in the 1979 climbing guidebook by Yosemite climbing pioneers Steve Roper and Allen Steck. Although McClatchie considers Pingora Peak a bucket-list climb and a beginner route, its remote location makes it deceptively difficult. For starters, would-be climbers need to hike about ten miles to reach its base, which requires a certain level of alpine fitness. The routes can also be hard to spot, so climbers need a trained eye, and its steep terrain requires technical skills and proper rope management. McClatchie, 34, has been climbing for over a decade and has climbed routes on Pingora Peak on three occasions between 2020 and 2022. He says that it’s not uncommon for people to get in sticky situations and need rescue. “I have witnessed parties on Pingora very late at night that were very clearly struggling to get down,” McClatchie said. “I don’t think I witnessed a rescue per se, but I’ve seen headlamps on the wall in the wee hours of the night in rainstorms.” “That’s the nature of alpine climbing,” McClatchie added. “Things can turn really quickly.”

item.title: No, You’re Not Imagining It. Bear Encounters Really Are on the Rise.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.51
Between 1990 and 2019, North American black and grizzly bears have killed 150 people (Photo: Scott Suriano/Getty Images) On the evening of August 31, a bear attacked a woman walking with her dog in Columbia Falls, Montana, a small town just outside of Glacier National Park. According to Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks (FWP), the woman sustained significant injuries and was transferred to a medical facility for treatment. The attack marks the latest in a long list of bear run-ins across North America this summer. Experts say that human-bear encounters have been higher in 2026 than in recent years. “Especially with black bears, we’ve definitely seen an uptick in their activity and subsequent conflict activity across the state,” Dan Thompson, large carnivore biologist with the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, told Outside. Bears have already killed two people this year. Anthony Pollio, 33, died while hiking in Glacier National Park in May. A black bear attacked and killed a New Mexico man in August, marking the state’s second fatal bear attack on record. A grizzly attacked two Yellowstone hikers, a Wyoming woman was bitten in the butt by a black bear, an Alaska woman fended off a grizzly using jiu-jitsu, and a black bear charged a group of students in Washington State. It seems the bears are everywhere. Thompson attributes the heightened bear activity to a one-two punch of weather extremes: an unusually low snowpack across the West last winter, followed by scorching summer temperatures. Together, those conditions have diminished the natural food sources bears rely on, including the berries, fruits, nuts, and grasses that make up the bulk of their diet. With less food available in the wild, more bears are venturing beyond their usual habitat and into neighborhoods in search of an easier meal. “Human-bear conflicts in general tend to increase when there are shortages of natural bear foods,” Frank van Manen, a bear expert and emeritus ecologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, told Outside. “It is possible that conflicts suddenly drop off if high-calorie foods that bears pursue in the fall are abundant. In areas where such foods are in low supply, human-bear conflicts may intensify.” Montana, home to nearly two-thirds of grizzly bears in the Lower 48, has reported 194 grizzly conflicts so far in 2026, and another 250 black bear-related incidents, according to Montana FWP data. “This year is panning out to be one of the worst natural food failure years on record,” Jamie Jonkel, Montana FWP bear conflict specialist, said in a statement. “Our regional bear team is working around the clock, and we are asking the public to be patient and to please be diligent with containing all attractants.” In Colorado, the state confirmed five black bear attacks amid an all-time high of more than 8,600 sightings, more than double the number of sightings in 2025. Connecticut wildlife officials reported that over 50 bears have entered homes. There have been at least 168 black bear incidents this year in Utah—also twice the amount from the previous year—and another 187 in New Mexico. Bear populations in some areas are also rebounding, moving beyond their recovery zones, and this year’s low food supply has only compounded those pressures. “There’s no silver bullet, no divine answer for why exactly,” Thompson said. “It’s a combination of factors: the lack of winter in other areas, moisture turning into a lot of heat, early blooms that froze and reduced the berry crop, and increased human use of these areas.” Vocabulary matters when you’re talking about bear data. Here’s how the experts distinguish between different events. Data suggests that brown bear attacks are rising around the world. According to a 2019 study, between 2000 and 2015 there were 183 attacks in North America, averaging 11 every year. Most of these victims were lone males recreating outside. Research on U.S. bear attacks is consistent with these numbers. Between 1990 and 2019, North American black and grizzly bears have killed at least 150 people, and more people have died in recent decades than a century ago. Scientists involved in the studies concluded that’s partly because far more people may be encountering bears. As remote bear territory diminishes, these encounters are even more likely to rise. Cody Miller, a wildlife scientist at Brigham Young University in Utah, wrote in his 2024 study that human–bear conflicts are still rare, but increasing at a steady rate because more people are hiking, camping, and hunting than ever before. Van Manen adds that more people in the landscape also increases the likelihood that bears encounter and pursue human foods, like garbage left behind at camp. Grizzlies account for more conflicts than black bears and are more likely to injure people, Miller concluded. Interestingly, though, black bear conflicts are more likely to be fatal. Most of these incidents began as surprise encounters, as with Pollio in Glacier. Van Manen cautions that although 2026 appears to be an unusually active year for encounters, it doesn’t necessarily mean that fatal bear attacks are on the rise—such a trend takes years of data to establish. “Because of the rarity of these events, comparisons of a single year with a ten-year average are not meaningful,” van Manen said. “Decadal comparisons for North America do not suggest distinct trends.” According to van Manen, grizzly bears killed 17 people in the United States during the 2010s, and 14 in the 2020s so far. American black bears, by comparison, killed ten people in the 2010s and 13 so far in the 2020s. Since 1892, researchers have documented 20 fatal attacks in the Greater Yellowstone area; some years have more, others less. “This is an example of how unpredictable these events are: there was a fatality in 1986 followed by a 25-year period with no fatal incidents and then several years with multiple incidents,” van Manen said. Nationwide tracking doesn’t exist—states hold the data—and establishing a full, nationwide picture of bear deaths is challenging. Chris Servheen, the former national grizzly bear recovery coordinator for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, told Outside that statistically speaking, a grizzly kills less than one person annually, on average. Even one death is a tragedy, and most fatal attacks are purely coincidental, van Manen adds. “These are chance events that are driven by human and bear numbers: in areas with increasing and expanding bear populations,” he said. “Combined with increases in recreational visits, the chance of a bear encounter that may end in a physical attack increases as well, however small that may be.” But all that could change as we head into the fall months. As more people move into bear country, and more bears come into towns looking for food, conflicts are sure to increase. Late summer and early autumn bring hyperphagia, a period during which bears spend almost all their time consuming calories to build fat reserves for winter. As more bears spend more time looking for food, the chances of people coming across them during fall hikes or bike rides increase. Nathaniel Bowersock is a biologist who spent nearly a decade working with bears in Yellowstone National Park. He is now a black bear specialist in Missouri and works with BearWise, a national program of the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies dedicated to mitigating human-bear conflict. He says the most important thing hikers can do is bring bear spray. “Bear spray continues to be shown to be an effective tool at deterring or lessening an encounter with a bear, both black bears and grizzly bears, and bear spray will work under many conditions, even on a windy day,” Bowersock told Outside. “In addition, bear spray has been found to be more effective than a firearm at deterring a bear encounter, and bear spray is easier to use than a firearm. Therefore, any time someone is looking to recreate in grizzly country, I strongly suggest they carry bear spray.” And if you see something, say something. “We have a lot of bears that don’t get reported until it’s too late, or until their behavior is at a level that we can’t tolerate from a human safety standpoint,” Thompson said. “Don’t let garbage be available. Don’t let food be available. Bring in pet food. When you’re camping, make sure you’re keeping a clean camp.”

item.title: Recent Research Says That Climbing Can Reduce Depression and Anxiety
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.48
(Photo: Canva) My eyes shot open two hours before my alarm, again, and the anxiety train that is my postpartum brain pulled out of the station right on schedule. I’m a journalist and Outside‘s former health history columnist, and I work full-time. I’m also a new parent. Naturally, my work hours and personal life are all over the place. Four months into motherhood, I find myself managing everything from moments of crushing anxiety to bouts of depression any time I question my parenting abilities. On top of that, as a runner and someone who loves to ski and do anything outdoors, I’m feeling a bit of cabin fever these days and trying to figure out when the hell I can get back on my workout schedule or do any kind of physical activity at all. That said, you can imagine my surprise—and subsequent elation—when I came across a study, published this year, where people with anxiety and depression climbed rocks to work through it. I interviewed the paper’s lead author and a psychologist who specializes in sports and performance. Here’s what they had to say. The study, published in the scientific journal BMC Medicine, is the latest from a German research team that has spent over a decade testing bouldering as therapy. Bouldering is a type of rock climbing done on small rock formations (or indoor rock walls) sans rope and harness. For safety, rocks are generally no more than 20 feet high. Researchers in this 2026 study randomly assigned 128 adults with diagnosed depression into three groups: one did structured bouldering therapy, another tried a newer talk therapy, and a third received standard care as a comparison. That newer talk therapy is called WISE-T, which stands for What’s Important: Schedule and Engage Therapy, and it focuses on identifying what actually matters to you and following through on it, instead of reacting to whatever feels most urgent. The goal of that therapy is to help combat symptoms that accompany depression, including anhedonia—the inability to feel joy or pleasure. In this study, bouldering involved climbing moderate heights, up to ten feet, without ropes or harnesses. Thick pads at the bottom broke falls. Each bouldering session involved three parts: a mindfulness exercise beforehand, the climbing portion, and a relaxation component at the end of class. The two therapy groups ran for ten weeks, once a week, in real settings: a bouldering gym for the bouldering therapy group and a psychiatric clinic for the WISE-T group, led throughout by trained therapists. Both WISE-T and bouldering therapy cut anxiety scores significantly compared with standard care, which barely changed over the same ten weeks. Depression, the study’s main focus, dropped in both groups. On average, people went from moderate depression to mild. Bouldering’s effect was considered moderate; the talk therapy’s was slightly larger, though the gap is small. What matters most is that two very different approaches, one physical, one purely cognitive, both worked. Self-efficacy also improved, most clearly in the talk therapy group. Self-efficacy refers to people’s belief in their ability to handle hard situations. The bouldering group’s effect on self-efficacy appeared, too, but only after some statistical untangling. As expected, only the bouldering group showed a jump in mindfulness during physical activity, and lead researcher Katharina Luttenberger has a theory as to why. “Thought can never be in the here and now, because thoughts necessarily always deal with the past or the future. Therefore, it makes perfect sense to me that mindfulness is fostered through physical activity rather than through cognitive engagement,” she told Outside. Because the participants were randomly assigned to groups, the results are more than a coincidence, but researchers can’t say that bouldering itself caused every improvement. Scientists can conclude, however, that there is an association between fewer depression symptoms, reduced anxiety, and bouldering therapy. The researchers have a clear explanation for why climbing specifically works: a boulder problem forces total, immediate attention. Every route is a specific puzzle you have to solve with your body, right now, leaving no spare processing power for anything else. That’s different from running or cycling, where your mind can wander for miles. Add real but manageable risk, a fall that’s expected, cushioned, and pretty safe, and you get practice handling uncertainty in a contained space. A 2025 survey on bouldering found that nearly three-quarters of American climbers said the sport had a real, positive effect on their mental health. Over 70 percent of 748 people surveyed said climbing was more effective at improving their mental state than medication, and nearly 65 percent said bouldering was better than therapy. Teresa Behrend Fletcher, a psychologist at Adler University who studies sports and human performance, explained that metaphors work in therapy because clients get stuck rehashing a problem the same way, and a metaphor forces a different angle. Bouldering works especially well for this, she said, because a client isn’t just imagining a solution; they’re finding one in real-time. Standing back and reading a route, then adjusting mid-climb when the first plan fails, mirrors the process of working through anything hard. As she put it, the goal is ensuring that “every problem has a solution,” Fletcher told Outside. A few limitations in Luttenberger’s study are worth noting. This study took place in one city, at one gym, and participants were employed and already getting some kind of treatment for their anxiety or depression. But the appeal here isn’t just the sport itself. It’s finding anything that demands your full attention long enough to interrupt rumination and anxious-thinking loops. Trail running a technical descent might do it. So might reading whitewater, or skiing a double black diamond trail. It’s not the rock that matters. It’s what engaging with the rock or other outdoor entity takes off your plate. When you’re trying to survive, your worries tend to fall away. Now, is bouldering therapy going to be a widespread method for alleviating anxiety and depression? Not quite. Luttenberger said that it depends on therapists’ qualifications and national regulations. “In Germany, for example, where the study took place, group psychotherapy is covered by health insurance, and under certain conditions, certified therapists can offer group sessions in various settings,” she said. One of the biggest hurdles in group bouldering psychotherapy, she said, is that “therapeutic climbing with a group of people with mental health issues is very demanding and should not be underestimated.” For it to be feasible and effective, “thorough training in all three areas—psychotherapy, climbing safety, and therapeutic climbing—is required.” I personally haven’t been bouldering, and I’m not claiming it would fix anything. But a researcher and a psychologist, working independently, landed on the same idea, and it’s got me thinking that heading to a climbing gym or even tackling a small boulder on my own might be that way out of my postpartum fog. Whether I climb or find time to get back on the running trails, my goal is to move my body in a way that pulls me out of my head for a while. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound Backpack Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.61
The Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound 55 Backpack is an ultralight backpack weighing 29.8 oz (819 g) made with Woven Dyneema fabric and Dyneema mesh. This new version is a substantial upgrade from the previous model, with more durable fabrics, a better frame system, and female-friendly (S-shaped) shoulder straps. Together, they make the pack much more comfortable and functional, enough so that existing Unbound owners should consider upgrading to the new model. - Color: Grey - Spec Weight: 29.8 oz (819 g) - Actual Weight: 29.8 oz (819 g) in a size large - Gender: Unisex - Volume: 55L internal storage, 9L external storage - Sizing: Multiple torso and hipbelt lengths - Frame: Contoured aluminum stay, foam back panel - Load lifters: None - Pockets: 6 (2 side, 1 front, 1 bottom, 2 hip belt) - Hydration Compatible: No - Material: Dyneema Woven Composite, 100D Dyneema Gridstop, Dyneema Stretch Mesh - Seam-taped: Yes - Pros: Tougher fabrics and mesh, effectively waterproof, good pockets, multiple torso lengths, excellent attachment points Backpack Pockets and Storage The Unbound 55 is a rolltop backpack that can be buckled together on top or along the sides using webbing straps, which are girth-hitched to the daisy chains along the sides so you can remove them if you don't need them. I prefer securing a roll top with them because I find that they provide better compression than just rolling the extension collar (the top of the pack) and buckling it on top. The top of the extension collar has a stiffener, making it easy to roll shut and helping it stay shut. The Unbound comes with huge side pockets that are great for storing multiple bottles, securing a tent along the side, and holding the bottom of a snowshoe if you hike in winter. The top of the side pockets has an elastic cinch cord for securing the contents. The Unbound does not have an internal hydration pocket or hydration ports, so you'll need to carry water in these pockets or in accessory sleeves attached to the shoulder straps. The hipbelt pockets are similarly large and can easily fit a Smartphone and snack bars or gloves. HMG expanded its hipbelt pocket size a few years ago, so this isn't a net new change. The pack also comes with two open stretch mesh pockets, one on the front and one on the bottom of the pack, which is a feature that's become popular with thru-hikers. The front mesh pocket is pretty unique: it has a top opening and a lower one about halfway down, held shut with elastic. It lets you access items at the base of the front pocket without unloading everything. For example, I keep my tent stakes at the base of the front stretch pocket, and this lets me access them easily. Both the front mesh pocket and the pocket at the base of the pack are made with highly durable Dyneema stretch mesh, since these zones experience considerable contact with the ground. The bottom pocket is a convenient place to store small snacks and trash, or hats and gloves, as long as you don't mind crushing the contents or getting them wet when you take the pack off and set it on wet ground. It has two openings: one on the right when facing forward and a small hole on the left, called a trash port, so you can stuff used wrappers into it. Backpack Frame and Suspension The Unbound 55 has dual contoured aluminum frame stays augmented with foam padding behind the shoulder straps for increased comfort. They terminate behind the lumbar pad at the base of the pack, providing much better load transfer to the hips. This is a major upgrade from the previous version, which had only one internal stay and is more comparable, in terms of load transfer and stability, to the HMG Southwest and Windrider backpacks, making the Unbound comparable to those mainstays of the Hyperlite product line in functionality and comfort. Take, for example, the UnBound hipbelt, which you tension by pushing the straps forward using what's called a Scherer cinch, named after Michael Scherer, who first designed it at Kelty. I get a much better hipwrap with the Unbound than the Southwest, which has been my backpack of choice for many years. The Unbound's shoulder straps, like HMG's other packs, are now S-shaped, making them more female-friendly. They are covered in front with daisy chains so you can easily attach accessory best-of-breed pockets, like the HMG shoulder strap pocket shown, bottle sleeves, or electronics to your shoulder straps. Hyperlite sells a full range of pack accessories. External Attachment Points and Compression The Unbound 55 has low-profile daisy chains sewn along the main compartment's side seams that you can use to secure bulky gear like fishing rods or packraft paddles to the sides of the pack. The pack comes with elastic cords for this purpose, but you can use your own instead. This is more difficult on Hyperlite's other packs, which offer less flexibility in strap placement. If you've ever lost a fishing rod because it's popped out of a backpack's side pocket, you'll really appreciate the intricate webs you can design to keep from losing precious cargo. Comparable Ultralight Backpacks w/Frames | Make / Model | Weight | Fabric | Price | |---|---|---|---| | Hyperlite Mtn Gear Southwest 55L | 29.8 / 845g | Dyneema Woven Composite | $395 | | Durston Kakwa 55L | 31.5 oz / 880g | Ultra 200X, UltraGrid | $279 | | Gossamer Gear Gorilla 50L | 31.9 oz / 904g | Robic Nylon | $275 | | Zpacks Arc Haul 60L | 20.9 oz / 593g | Ultra 100X | $399 | | Granite Gear Crown 3 60L | 32.6 oz / 1040g | Robic Nylon | $260 | | Osprey Exos Pro 55 | 34.6 oz / 981g | Robic Nylon | $330 | | ULA Ultra Circuit SV 48L | 35.8 oz / 1015g | Ultra 200X, Ultra400X | $380 | | REI Flash 55L | 45 oz / 1276g | Robic Nylon | $229 | | Atom Packs Notch EP40 | 29.6 oz / 840g | Ecopack EPX200, EPX400 | $303 | | SWD UL Long Haul 50 | 30.2 oz / 856g | Ultra 200X | $379 | Recommendation The Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound 55 is an excellent ultralight backpack for multi-day backpacking trips, excelling across a wide range of trail conditions and gear needs. It differs from Hyperlite's other backpacks in pocket size and placement, offers a more adjustable hip belt, and provides more flexible external attachments. This new version also represents a major upgrade in two key components: a switch from a single aluminum stay to dual stays and the use of woven Dyneema as the pack fabric, making it significantly tougher and abrasion-resistant. The new grey-silver color is also pretty cool. The upgraded Unbound 55 is so impressive that owners of the previous version should consider upgrading if their existing pack is nearing the end of its life. It also wouldn't surprise me if the Unbound becomes the most popular pack in Hyperlite's backpacking line, even outshining the Southwest and Windrider backpacks, because the hipbelt is easier to tighten and fit and the pack is more functional with no added weight gain. Disclosure: Hyperlite Mountain Gear donated a backpack for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Thanks for the review. Could you easily get a bear canister into it? Yes, of course. Anyone you want, vertically. It’s a 55L pack. But here’s a jedi tip – pack your food/smellables in a plastic bag inside your pack and carry the empty canister under the Y strap on top of the pack. At night, put your food into the bear canister. This makes it much easier to carry a bear canister because it won’t be top heavy and throw you off balance without losing pack volume or increasing gear weight. I like that Jedi tip, thanks!

item.title: Gossamer Gear “The Free” Freestanding Tent Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.23
The Gossamer Gear The Free is a freestanding, double-wall ultralight tent made with Robic nylon that weighs 29.8 oz. It has a single front vestibule and requires two multi-segment aluminum tent poles for setup. While it is very lightweight, the tent is quite narrow inside, with a tapered footprint and sloping walls that can feel claustrophobic. The designers clearly optimized for weight over livability, with mixed results. - Freestanding (inner tent first) - Trail Weight: 29.8 oz total / 845 g - Total Weight: 33.02 oz / 935.8 g (including stuff sacks, stakes) - Minimum tent stakes to pitch: 1 (door) 5-6 recommended - Interior Dimensions: head end: 34″ / 86.4 cm; foot end: 21.5″ / 54.6 cm; length: 86″ / 218.4 cm; height: 39″ / 99.1 cm - Bathtub floor: 7″ deep / 178 cm - Pockets: 2 – ceiling, corner - Seam-sealed: Yes - Materials: 15D Recycled Robic fabric with a 20D dope-dyed ripstop SIL/PU coating (1200 mm) - Hydrostatic head: 4,923 mm The Free is a freestanding double-wall tent with a separate inner tent and rainfly, where the inner tent must be set up first. It has two tent poles joined by a central pivoting hub that hooks onto the inner tent ceiling, while the rest attaches to the poles using plastic clips. When setting up the inner tent, it's easiest to stake out the corners before inserting the pole ends into the corner hardware. Once that's done, you can pick up the inner tent and move it to a different location as desired, but trying to insert the poles without a fixed corner is awkward at best, and downright comical if anyone is watching. The inner tent has a directional pitch, with a wider head end (34″) and a narrower foot end (21.5″). The inner has a high bathtub floor with a D-shaped door. While the foot end is narrower than many non-tapered or wide inflatable sleeping pads, you can still fit one if you don't mind losing some bathtub-floor height. The inner tent is 86″ long, but the wall slopes in noticeably. When I sat up inside (I'm 5'10”), my shoulders touched the inner tent's side walls; I measured the width here at 12″. While you're less likely to experience internal condensation transfer in a double-wall tent, the Free is pretty narrow and feels like the walls are closing in, making the tent feel more like sleeping in a bivy than a tent. This happens because there isn't a horizontal strut keeping the two overhead crossing poles separated, so they sag toward each other and reduce the tent's effective interior space. I tried fashioning a cross brace like this with sticks, as similar tents from other manufacturers do, but the fly fabric is so slippery that they slid right off. I suspect adding an extra pole component would bump the shelter weight up over 2 pounds, but it'd be worth it to improve the tent's livability. There are two pockets on the inside of the tent, one in the door-side corner of the head end and the second in the ceiling. The corner pocket is triangular and should be used with caution. Every time I put my glasses in, they simply slid out, over and over. There's a gear loft overhead and a large plastic hook on the ceiling, and you'd be better off stowing or hanging delicate items from them instead. The rainfly drapes over the inner tent and secures to the corner hardware used to stake out the inner tent. There's no way to attach the fly to the pole set, again using tiny toggles or Velcro as provided in other weather-worthy tents. I didn't test the tent in high winds, but I'd expect some flapping. There's a vestibule zipper with a wide fabric flap over the front vestibule to prevent a deluge of rain (onto you) when you unzip the tent in the pouring rain. You can roll back both halves of the vestibule and secure them with toggles. Many competitive ultralight tents now use magnets instead of toggles. You'll appreciate the difference in ease of use when it starts to rain, and you struggle to undo a toggle while staying inside the inner tent. Assessement I've used and recommended Gossamer Gear products for a long time, but I'd pass on The Free tent. The Free would be more competitive with a perpendicular cross pole between its existing two tent poles to create more vertical sidewalls inside. It's too confining now. Several freestanding double-wall tents in the same weight range offer far better internal livability, like the MSR Freelite 1 (26 oz) or the Big Agnes Copper Spur 1P (32 oz). I'd recommend adding them to your short list instead. Disclosure: Gossamer Gear donated a tent for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. I’m a Gossamer Gear fan and have several packs. I was going to get The One until they made it smaller. The Free reminds me of the Exped solo from a few years ago, which passed into the sunset. I don’t know what GG was thinking when this tent was brought to market. Where is the upside? IMHO this tent and the big company tents don’t come close to the Durston X-Dome 1+ on features for a similar price. The fly first pitch is a game changer for me. Yes, you may have to wait a while on an order. But you can choose carbon or aluminum poles. However, the MSR, Big Agnes and Nemo tents can be found on sale several time a year which is a big plus. a short answer and a long answer: 1) Gossamer Gear is a backpack company not a tent company, just a six moon designs is a tent company and not a backpack company. 2) Some of the mid-size cottages like Gossamer Gear and Hyperlite are hell bent on making and selling as many things as possible in their online stores, regardless of quality because it is a gold rush out there for ultralight gear. I think they shipped this despite its flaws because they needed it out before the holiday season, knowing that people would buy the “brand” and not the tent. There may also have been a calculation that are enough large websites and Youtube reviewers out there who think they can make money on affiliate sales by giving it a good review or merely mentioning it, that the dissenting voices will be drowned out. Think Wirecutter. Then, as is Gossamer’s standard pattern of behavior, they’ll fix it in version two. It’s also worth noting that Gossamer Gear has hired a bunch of people who are not original staff and aren’t necessarily experienced backpackers. That may also have dilluted an appreciation for the finer points of livability. How does the new fabric compare to prior versions of the One and Two– any noticeable improvement? more slippery.

item.title: ‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern Spain
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.14
Once upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name. They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today in Somiedo natural park – one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988. Setting his scope on a tripod in a steep-angled pasture, Frechilla spots a bear almost as soon as we start looking. A juvenile, apparently, which means the animal is old enough to be foraging alone, but it’s still too small, and too far away, for him to tell if it’s a male or female. Another bear-spotter standing near us seems more willing to take a guess. “Ooh, look at his little ears,” she says delightedly, beaming behind binoculars. No expert myself, I watch that distant fuzzy shape move across the viewfinder and along the sharp ridges opposite, blinking in and out of sight like a cursor on the trend line of a graph. I’m not sure that we are close enough to call this an encounter, but it is an experience. The sun drops behind the peaks; the birds sing a dusk chorus in the birches and oaks; cowbells ring through the valley from the dairy herds that help this region of so-called “Green Spain” look and sound like the Swiss Alps. It gets cold at night up here, and it’s been known to snow in summer, though my own visit in late spring sees the mountaintops looking whiter than anyone around here can remember so deep into May. That weather, and the sheer calorific spend of living and working at a median altitude of 1,300 metres, has made the traditional cuisine much sturdier here than elsewhere in Spain. Down at the village inn, Casa Miño, we share a bottle of regional cider and a cachopo (beef fillet topped with serrano ham, peppers and goat cheese, and pounded into a single solid unit the size of a solar panel). I want fabada, too, the famous Asturian stew of white beans, pork belly and blood sausage. Frechilla says it’s a winter dish, customarily eaten for lunch – too heavy for the body to process later in the day. But I would order fabada at midnight in a heatwave, and keep eating it even while they loaded me into the ambulance. The bears, meanwhile, don’t have much to feed on at the moment. They only woke from hibernation a few weeks ago, explains Alicia Madrid the next day, on a forest trail above the century-old hydroelectric power station at La Malva. A biologist with the conservation group Fundación Oso Pardo, Madrid tells me that Cantabrian bears don’t hibernate as long or deeply as other brown bears and are generally smaller and lighter than American grizzlies. “They’re adapted to this terrain, and they can’t be too heavy because they have to climb a lot,” she says. Their paw prints in the mud look big enough to me, and the bite marks where they chewed clumps of long grasses, and the hairs shed where they scratched their backs against trees. Madrid shows us, too, the hefty rocks they overturned looking for insects. Further into the summer, there’ll be plenty of berries, acorns, chestnuts and maybe some meaty carrion to fatten them up. The foundation has played a major role in the regrowth of bear populations, building bio-corridors with strategic placements of trees and bushes full of all the things they like to eat. Another key factor is the hunting ban, introduced in 1973. The trick now, says Madrid, is coaxing isolated cohorts to breed with other groups and boost genetic diversity. Also: managing the tourists who come to see them, and balancing ecological imperatives against financial incentives. Later, after a long hike through the Valley of the Lake to reach the aptly named Lake of the Valley, I overhear Frechilla fielding the related concerns of two local women. Against a backdrop of blue sky, bright wildflowers and silver waters, the women seem to argue that conservation efforts amount to commercial exploitation. Frechilla gently insists that Somiedo natural park is a model of good practice in Spain. Much of the bears’ territory is closed to the public, and spotting expeditions are only permitted in the company of licensed guides. Nature tourism, he says, keeps villagers in jobs where farming culture cannot, and is proving vastly more sustainable than hunting bears for sport. As for protecting humans, there has been only one bear attack in recent memory, on an elderly lady whose evening stroll led her between a mother and cubs. She survived. For now, at least, most residents seem willing to share the bears with outsiders. That evening, a small crowd gather by the side of a winding back road near Saliencia, some sitting comfortably on camping chairs with spotting scopes in their hands. Everyone is watching a large male bear – so big and so close that they don’t need the viewing equipment – as he lopes across a meadow to take a quick splash in the river. Another male is spotted in the treeline above, and the two circle each other at a distance for a while. There is some speculation that they might fight for this turf, and a man with two leashed greyhounds seems ready to take bets on it. Frechilla shakes his head. “Maybe later in the season, when they’ve gained enough weight.” These bears are doing better now, but it’s still a tough life. The reality of their ongoing baby boom is that only 30% of juveniles will survive on their own, after a year of maternal supervision. This is surely why I find it so moving when we follow reports of another sighting in the twilight: a mother and her two young cubs have been seen climbing a slope called El Diente, or “The Tooth”. It’s getting dark and cold, but we can see them through the scopes, about a mile away from us across the high mountain pass at La Peral. I watch the mother bear waiting and cajoling as needed while the siblings struggle up the vertical planes of rock like toddlers trying to climb a baby gate. On the ridgeline, they turn to silhouettes, play-fighting against a white sky. They disappear over the far side, but then a little one comes back, seeming to wave goodbye with both front paws in the air. I remember a story I read to my daughter once, which put a poignant time limit on the usual fairytale ending: “And they all lived happily together, for as long as they could.” The trip was provided by the Spanish Tourist Office, Turismo Asturias and Casa Miño in Pola de Somiedo. Bear-spotting tours with nature guide Luis Frechilla can be organised through Wild Spain Travel. For more information on the Cantabrian brown bear and related conservation efforts, visit Fundación Oso Pardo Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.85
Sometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45. There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.” It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away. I arrive the previous night, a little disoriented, whizzing past unlit buildings, huge brick structures like Victorian factories. “Are we in the city yet?” I ask. The taxi driver gives me a quizzical look. “Yes, this is Łódź.” I note the pronunciation, like “wudge”. I glimpse five-storey blocks, tree-lined streets, a tramline. “I could never live anywhere else,” he adds. A huge blue graffito is caught in the headlights, like a monstrous alien creature. “Why?” I ask, but we are already pulling up outside an immense red-brick building, my hotel, and he never answers my question. The reception area is huge, with a strange scalloped ceiling in red brick that hints at a previous incarnation as a factory. This is my first visit to Łódź, a city about 75 miles (120km) south-west of Warsaw. My interest has been piqued by a list of notable people associated with the place. It features an astonishing number of Oscar-winning or nominated film directors connected to the city: Andrzej Wajda (The Promised Land), Roman Polanski (The Pianist), Paweł Pawlikowski (Ida), Agnieszka Holland (Europa Europa), Krzysztof Kieślowski (Three Colours trilogy) and Zbigniew Rybczyński (Tango). But under the bonnet there is a vast array of talent in acting, production and technical excellence. The city’s film school is responsible, of course, but Łódź itself features as a setting, too, notably in David Lynch’s Inland Empire and Wajda’s masterpiece The Promised Land. Łódź, I had decided, must be fascinating. Any visit starts with Piotrkowska Street, the longest shopping street in Europe at about 2½ miles. My guide, Anna, takes me through Plac Wolności (Freedom Square), where a dance festival is in progress, with hooded hip‑hoppers rubbing shoulders with troupes of line dancers and girls in colourfully embroidered traditional dress. This is a city where music and dance are never far away. We dodge down a side alley and emerge in a striking art installation – an entire street, Pasaż Róży (Rosa’s Passage), covered in mirrors by the artist Joanna Rajkowska. Back on the main pedestrianised route, the mix of ancient and modern continues: 19th‑century porticoed palaces adorned with colourful graffiti. I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. “It was not too badly damaged,” she says. “Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.” There is no medieval heart, no ornate houses like in Wrocław or Kraków. What Łódź possesses is an impressive array of 19th-century factories, mostly textiles, built to show off their owners’ power, wealth and architectural aspirations. Now, this heritage has become a stunning example of urban regeneration. We turn into OFF Piotrkowska, a complex of beautiful old textile mills reborn as a hive of small businesses. There are lots of vibrant restaurants and bars, but Anna wants to show me a shop that she likes: Pan Tu Nie Stał. “It was a saying in communist times: ‘You’re not in the queue.’ We said it to people trying to push in,” Anna says. This is the spot to pick up a T-shirt featuring Soviet combine harvesters or some Czas Pokaże (Time Will Tell) socks. The shop says a lot about the Polish attitude to communist times: none of the maudlin ostalgie of East Germany; this nostalgia comes with healthy dashes of colour and humour. It did all start, however, with a disaster. The old mills had survived two world wars, but died in the economic collapse after communism ended in 1989. “Everything closed down,” says Anna. “We call that time the transformacja. It was very hard.” We stroll into the Manufaktura area, once the site of a vast textile business started by a local scrap metal dealer, Izrael Poznański, in 1872, and now another beautifully restored collection of red-brick buildings housing restaurants, bars, shops and the fascinating Museum of the Factory. Next door is the palace that Poznański built, a neo-baroque monstrosity of bulging wealth, now the city museum. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Łódź became part of the Russian empire, a melting pot of German, Jewish, Polish and Russian influences. In the 1870s, Poznański was one of a group of men who saw the potential of steam power. They imported looms from England and were soon amassing unimaginable wealth, constructing a city of handsome red-brick factories, the core of which still remains. The Museum of the Factory houses a collection of working looms that date back to the 1880s. Only four machines are ever turned on due to noise pollution laws – in the old days, one factory might have had hundreds. This was the city of the deaf, but the deafest of all were the bosses, oblivious to the terrible hardships of their workforce, from the founders through to their communist successors. When Wajda came to these mills in the early 1970s, planning The Promised Land, he needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming. The tired faces, the crashing looms, the heat and the dust – it was all very much like 1880. Is that your favourite film, I ask Anna? She shakes her head. “Cold War by Pawlikowski,” she says. “I love that film.” This 2018 masterpiece is the story of a tragic love affair conducted across the Iron Curtain in the years following the second world war. Based on the lives of Pawlikowski’s parents, it is dark and sensuous, full of great music and dance. Pawlikowski has used Łodż as a location. We move on to the Museum of Cinematography, a tour de force that warrants some preparation (watch films by Polish directors). They have everything from early working equipment to props from the most recent Oscar triumphs. By the time I get to the end, I have only a few minutes to rush to the Central Museum of Textiles. There I find a technician, Przemysław, about to start up a 1893 Greenwood loom. He’s a former policeman with a few tales to tell, but right now one question is bothering me. “Why did film-making succeed so brilliantly in this city of textiles?” I ask him. He taps the cast iron loom and chuckles. “I’ll show you.” With the flick of a switch, the loom begins to clank and turn. The noise is incredible. Przemysław is moving around, adjusting and calibrating, his face concentrated. I see the spools of thread begin to unwind, the shuttle dashing back and forth, the warp and weft rhythmically rising and falling. The different colours, each no more than a thin line, but magically coming together. And from the lip of the machine spills a beautiful multicoloured cloth. Przemysław looks at me and raises a questioning eyebrow. “Like weaving a story, right?” The trip was provided by the Polish Tourism Organisation, with Holiday Extras lending travel support in car parking, insurance, airport transfers and hotels

item.title: You can now go through TSA without a plane ticket at these airports
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.28
You can now go through TSA without a plane ticket at these airports The Transportation Security Administration now wants you to visit the airport without a plane ticket. Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks changed airport security and largely put an end to non-ticketed visitors meeting loved ones at the gate, the TSA is rolling out a new program welcoming non-ticketed visitors at 13 airports. The program, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck, invites non-travelers with TSA PreCheck status and Known Traveler Numbers to apply for an airport day pass and use the dedicated TSA PreCheck lanes for expedited entry to the airport. "This new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way," TSA said in the program announcement, adding that the program brings back "the moments that once defined air travel." The program could be particularly useful for people who want to help family members navigate the airport. Parents could accompany children all the way to their departure gate, while family members could escort older relatives through security or meet them at the gate when they arrive. How it works Gateside by TSA PreCheck is free and is open to TSA PreCheck members and those with Known Traveler Numbers. To use the program, you'll need to apply one to three days before your planned visit, log in using your Login.gov account (or create one), enter your personal information on the form and wait for approval. Kids are welcome to join you, but be sure to enter their information on your reservation. Once approved, you'll need to bring a Real ID or other acceptable form of ID to a PreCheck lane at the airport and be prepared to log in to the application portal to show the TSA officer your approval status. Keep in mind that TSA says screenshots or printouts of your approval status won't be accepted for this program. For now, the Gateside by TSA PreCheck program is only available at 13 airports, with more promised by TSA in the coming months. If you don't have TSA PreCheck or know that your membership will soon be renewed, here's the TPG guide to everything you need to know about TSA PreCheck and some ways to get free or discounted TSA membership. Airports rolling out Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) Gateside by TSA versus other airport gate pass programs At least 20 airports already welcome non-ticketed guests to apply for gate passes to visit the non-secure side of the airport. These programs go by different names at each airport; for example, there's the Hopkins Hang Out Pass at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) and the Wingmate Pass at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). These programs differ from Gateside: While they do run an applicant's name through the TSA database, anyone can apply for a pass, and no PreCheck membership is required. And for these gate pass programs, using the TSA PreCheck lanes to enter the airport is prohibited. Related: The best credit cards for TSA PreCheck and Global Entry Some of those gate pass programs also differ in that applications for same-day access are often permitted, the application windows can be much longer, and screenshots and printouts of approved passes are often allowed. Here's a list of airports with their own gate pass programs: - Albuquerque International Airport (ABQ) - Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) - Kansas City International Airport (MCI) - Louis Armstrong International Airport (MSY) - Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Nashville International Airport (BNA) - Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) - San Antonio International Airport (SAT) - Tulsa International Airport (TUL) - John Wayne Airport (SNA) in California - Ontario International Airport (ONT) in California - Capital Regional International Airport (LAN) in Michigan - Tri-Cities Airport (PSC) in Washington - San Francisco International Airport (SFO) - Orlando International Airport (MCO) - Shreveport Regional Airport (SHV) in Louisiana - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Tampa International Airport (TPA) Note that two of the above airports — SAN and DTW — are also on the Gateside by TSA PreCheck list. We checked with the airports to see whether anything about their gate passes will change. Matt Morawski, director of communications and external affairs at DTW, said the DTW Destination Pass is available to anyone who meets the program requirements and has a valid government-issued ID. "We do not anticipate that the Gateside by TSA PreCheck program will have any impact on our DTW Destination Pass program," Morawski said. "We're pleased to continue offering this safe and convenient option for our customers." As for SAN, the airport's public information officer, Nicole Hall, said: "While both programs offer a similar experience by allowing access to the gate area without a boarding pass, they operate independently of one another, and there are some differences." She noted that TSA's Gateside program is only available to TSA PreCheck members, while the SAN Pass program works with TSA to approve applicants to use the normal (non-PreCheck) TSA security checkpoint line. "The timeline for requesting passes also differs between the programs," Hall said. "Our SAN Pass Program allows applicants to apply for the SAN Pass as early as seven days prior to their visit date and as late as the day of the visit." Bottom line Gateside by TSA PreCheck brings back an airport experience that largely disappeared more than two decades ago: the ability to accompany loved ones all the way to the gate even when you aren't flying yourself. Beyond meeting friends during layovers or taking advantage of airport dining and shopping, the program could be particularly valuable for families who want to accompany children or older relatives through the airport. And unlike existing airport visitor-pass programs, eligible Gateside visitors get the added benefit of using TSA PreCheck lanes to get through security.

item.title: TSA liquids rule: What to know about 3-1-1 before you head to the airport
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.04
TSA liquids rule: What to know about 3-1-1 before you head to the airport Editor's Note It's the rule every passenger has to consider when packing for a flight. For 20 years now, the Transportation Security Administration has enforced rules on the liquids passengers can bring in carry-on bags. This policy is the reason you can't bring a full-size bottle of shampoo or sunscreen through a TSA checkpoint. It's one of the biggest reasons bags get pulled for secondary screening. Last year, the TSA stopped requiring flyers to take off their shoes, but the liquids rule remains one of the biggest hurdles travelers still face when passing through security. But what exactly are the TSA liquid rules, and why do they exist? And, most importantly, what does this mean for packing ahead of your next trip? Here's a quick rundown. TSA liquids rules: Why do they exist? The TSA's restrictions on liquids date back to 2006. In the wake of a thwarted terrorism plot overseas, the agency started restricting the liquids, gels and aerosols passengers could bring in their carry-on baggage. Scores of other countries around the world put similar policies in place in the name of aviation security. What is the TSA's 3-1-1 rule? The TSA's ban on liquids — or at least large quantities of them — is governed by what's known as the "3-1-1 rule." The decades-old policy states that: - Liquids must be in containers no larger than 3.4 ounces, or roughly 100 milliliters (that's the "3"). - All containers must be placed in one clear, quart-size plastic bag ("1"). - Each passenger is only allowed one such plastic bag ("1"). These rules govern liquids, gels and aerosol products ranging from toothpaste to shampoo, conditioner, mouthwash and sunscreen — among other products. Liquid products larger than 3.4 ounces must be placed in a checked bag. That applies even to those large shampoo containers with just a tiny bit of shampoo left, per TSA policy. Exceptions to the TSA's 3-1-1 policy There are a few exceptions, though. The TSA will allow you to bring "medically necessary" liquids, gels and aerosols in reasonable quantities for your flight. However, you must declare those items to security officers at the checkpoint for inspection. The agency asks travelers with larger amounts of medically necessary liquids to remove them from the carry-on bag and place them in a bin or bowl. The TSA has a variety of alternative screening methods it can use. What can you bring through a TSA checkpoint? You can bring creamy cheeses, liquid chocolate, liquid coffee, creamy dips and spreads, gravy, honey, hummus, ice cream, jam, jelly, juice, syrup, peanut butter, salad dressing, sauce, salsa, soda, soup and yogurt as long as they are in a container of less than 3.4 ounces, according to the TSA. You can bring your water bottle with you — as long as it's empty. This can also be a great way to save money at the airport, since many now have postsecurity filling stations for reusable water bottles. When in doubt, consult the TSA's list of what you can carry through the airport and check with your airline. Or, better yet, download the MyTSA app. It contains a "Can I Bring?" section, allowing you to look up items and find out whether they're allowed outright, restricted to 3.4 ounces, permitted only in a checked bag, permitted only in a carry-on bag or prohibited altogether. Could 3-1-1 finally go away? While the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids rules remain in place, there's reason to wonder how long they'll be around. The U.K. has begun a long-planned rollback of its liquids rules. And after the TSA ended its long-standing "shoes-off" policy in 2025, the Trump administration signaled that the liquids restrictions could be next ... someday. "We're exploring technologies that might allow us to bring water bottles again through checkpoints," newly appointed TSA administrator David Cummins told Congress during his summer 2026 confirmation hearing. So, abide by the rules for now. But stay tuned.
